For LTT-9779, we measure a broadband granulation amplitude of σ$=53.8^{+4.1}_{-4.0}$ppm at a timescale of τ$=4.8^{+1.5}_{-1.3}$min. For WASP-121, we measure σ$=59.3\pm4.3$ppm and τ$=6.3^{+2.1}_{-1.8}$min. We also measure peak oscillation frequencies of ν$=3382^{+166}_{-191}μ$Hz and $1649^{+55}_{-69}μ$Hz in the bandpass-integrated power spectra of LTT-9779 and WASP-121, respectively. In the spectroscopic fits, we find $σ$ decreases with wavelength. Our results demonstrate a new observational window on short-timescale stellar variability and provides a way to characterize chromatic stellar noise in transit light curves.

Title: Harnessing Generative UI for Education: Tailored Learning Interactives
Authors: Alisa Kovshov, Anisha Choudhury, Anna Iurchenko, Amy Keeling, Avinatan Hassidim, Ayelet Shasha Evron, Ayça Çakmakli, Diana Akrong, Femi Olanubi, Gal Elidan, Ian Li, Ido Lerer, Katherine Chou, Lidan Hackmon, Michal Gordon, Nir Kerem, Niv Efron, Preeti Singh, Rena Levitt, Rotem Yulzary, Shlomi Ben Shimon, Sophie Allweis, Tracey Lee-Joe, Tzvika Stein, Yaniv Carmel, Yael Haramaty, Yishay Mor, Yossi Matias, Yuri Lev
Affiliations: Google (United States)
Abstract: It is well established that students learn best through active engagement, particularly via interactive experiences tied to real-world concepts. Creating such experiences, however, typically requires labor-intensive design, costly development, and continuous teacher guidance to achieve measurably effective outcomes. Recent advances in generative UI open the door for a future of practice where the creation of tailored interactive experiences is automated. However, off-the-shelf models lack optimization for pedagogical precision and learning principles, often yielding unsatisfactory results for complex pedagogical constructs. To address these limitations, we present learning interactives, a structured framework leveraging the generative UI capabilities of Gemini to construct effective customized interactive simulations. We evaluate our approach through both an initial study with educators as well as a pedagogical rating of a varied set of simulations by expert teachers.

Title: Human-AI Productivity Paradoxes: Modeling the Interplay of Skill, Effort, and AI Assistance
Authors: Ali Aouad, Thodoris Lykouris, Huiying Zhong
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly adopted in the workplace and in education, yet the empirical evidence on AI's impact remains mixed across different operating contexts. We propose a model of human-AI interaction to better understand and analyze several mechanisms by which AI affects productivity. In our setting, human agents with varying skill levels exert utility-maximizing effort to produce certain task outcomes with AI assistance. We find that incorporating endogeneity in skill development or AI unreliability can induce a productivity paradox: increased levels of AI assistance may degrade productivity, leading to potentially significant shortfalls. We construct interpretable measures that characterize when the productivity paradox occurs. Moreover, we examine the long-term distributional effect of AI on skill, and demonstrate that skill polarization can emerge in steady state. We identify an effort-skill non-monotonicity condition under which skill polarization emerges.

Title: Hybrid Momentum Methods for Optimizing Deep Learning Models
Authors: Haifeng Xu, Yijin Ren, Chenyu Zhou, Qi Deng, Dongdong Ge, Yinyu Ye
Affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics; Columbia University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract: Momentum is central to stochastic optimization in deep learning, including the training of large language models. Classical momentum methods typically rely on a fast exponential moving average (EMA) scheme, which discounts past gradients on a fixed timescale and may underweight older gradients that remain informative. This creates a trade-off between retaining long-term history and adapting to recent changes. We introduce Hybrid Momentum (HyM), which combines a linearly weighted average of past gradients with a geometrically discounted fast momentum. The former assigns weights proportional to the gradients' iteration indices and retains a growing span of history, while the latter emphasizes recent gradients. This hybrid construction is modular and can be combined with adaptive preconditioning and other update transformations. In particular, we propose HyMUON, which applies Newton--Schulz orthogonalization to the hybrid direction. Illustrative examples and controlled experiments demonstrate the benefits of combining gradient information across these two timescales. Across image classification, machine translation, and language modeling, HyM and HyMUON match or improve upon strong baselines. HyMUON improves over Muon on IWSLT14, and in both the 100k- and 600k-step GPT-2 124M OpenWebText regimes. For LLaMA-1.3B pretraining on C4, HyMUON achieves a final validation loss of 2.777, compared with 2.903 for Muon.

Title: Impossibility of No-Regret in Multi-Agent Bidding
Authors: Zongjun Yang, Rachitesh Kumar, Christian Kroer
Abstract: We consider $T$ repeated second-price auctions across $n$ pacing bidders with i.i.d. item arrivals, and show that it is computationally impossible for all bidders to achieve no-regret simultaneously while satisfying their respective budget or return-on-investment constraints. Therefore, in the prominent internet auction systems where buyers simultaneously deploy pacing algorithms or automated bidding agents, we cannot hope to achieve joint no-regret guarantees in general. We establish a deterministic relationship that high variance in online bidding systems implies high regret. By showing that one can extract a pacing equilibrium from a low-variance system, we prove PPAD-hardness of attaining joint no-regret. For several widely used bidding algorithms, we also show evidence from dynamical systems and numerical simulations that they can indeed display high-variance behavior through cycling, even on simple market instances.

Title: Improved Approximation Guarantees for Periodic-Review Stochastic Inventory Control
Authors: Danny Segev
Affiliations: Tel Aviv University
Abstract: In periodic-review stochastic inventory control, replenishment policies must balance holding and backlogging costs while responding to uncertain demands and evolving forecasts that may be arbitrarily correlated and nonstationary. In this general information setting, Levi, P{á}l, Roundy, and Shmoys (Mathematics of Operations Research 2007) established that the fully adaptive optimum can be approximated within factor $2$, which had remained the best-known performance guarantee since then. Their marginal cost accounting and dual-balancing framework made this comparison possible without computing optimal decisions across future trajectories, opening a broad research program on approximation algorithms for stochastic inventory systems. We break this long-standing barrier for periodic-review stochastic inventory control, showing how to compete against the fully adaptive benchmark within factor $\frac{ e }{ e-1 } \approx 1.582$ while retaining general demand correlations and evolving forecasts. We attain these advances by discovering a structural connection between marginal inventory accounting and weighted stopping problems, where each unit's conditional holding charge forms a supermartingale, while postponing its order incurs a history-dependent backlog charge. To leverage the random thresholding approach of Ma and Tzamos (ICML 2023) in this context, we develop a potential-function analysis, leading to an $\frac{ e }{ e-1 }$-approximation with respect to any unit's stopping problem. Subsequently, our common-threshold policy coordinates these marginal decisions into a global replenishment policy without additional loss.

Title: Improving Entrepreneurial Skills by Practicing with AI
Authors: Amir Globerson, Anisha Choudhury, Anna Iurchenko, Avinatan Hassidim, Cathy Cheung, E. Kim, Femi Olanubi, Gabby Espinosa, Gaby Andrews, Gal Elidan, Hannah Lieber, Hairong Mu, Katherine Chou, Nir Kerem, Niv Efron, Rajvi Kapadia, Rena Levitt, Rotem Yulzary, Shashank Agarwal, Tracey Lee-Joe, Victor Martinez, Yael Haramaty, Yishay Mor, Yossi Matias
Affiliations: Google (United States); Network For Teaching Entrepreneurship
Abstract: Durable skills like critical thinking, creativity, and collaboration are essential for innovation, yet teaching them remains difficult. In this work, we focus on the entrepreneurial domain, where these skills and others are required, and ask whether AI can be used as a tool for improving entrepreneurial proficiency. As a first step towards this challenge, we present an extension of Vantage, a platform developed at Google Research, adapted to serve as an interactive practice environment for entrepreneurship. Vantage pairs students with simulated AI peers engineered to navigate realistic business scenarios and challenge learners to exercise key skills. In a randomized controlled trial (RCT) embedded in summer entrepreneurship programs run by The Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE), students using Vantage scored significantly higher on their Capstone Business Plans than control students with access to standard AI tools. These preliminary findings suggest that orchestrated AI peers can meaningfully support short-term performance on tasks requiring complex, durable skills.

Title: Improving Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring by Differentiating Human Tutor Roles Based on Student Needs
Authors: Ashish Gurung, Ge Gao, Jordan Gutterman, Danielle R. Thomas, Shivang Gupta, Lee Branstetter, Emma Brunskill, Vincent Aleven, Kenneth R. Koedinger
Affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University; Stanford University
Abstract: Hybrid human-AI tutoring, where technology and humans jointly facilitate student learning, can be more beneficial than AI-only tutoring. However, preliminary evidence suggests that lower-performing students derive greater benefit from human-AI tutoring than higher-performing students. As such, this study evaluates whether a differentiated tutoring policy can effectively support both groups: human tutors initiate support for lower-performing students, while higher-performing students receive reactive, on-demand support. Using their within-grade median state test scores, we assigned 635 students (grades 5-8) to receive proactive (< median) or reactive ($\geq$ median) tutoring. Using a DiDC design, we compare outcomes across two time periods: fall (AI-only tutoring) and spring (proactive-reactive human-AI tutoring). This quasi-experimental design isolates the effects of proactive-reactive tutoring approaches by comparing the discontinuity in spring outcomes to the fall, where no such discontinuity existed. Using data around the cutoff (Imbens-Kalyanaraman criterion), we find significant overall improvements from human-AI tutoring compared to AI-only baseline: 25% increase in time on task, 36% in skill proficiency, and 61% in academic growth (standardized MAP test). Between proactive and reactive tutoring, we find comparable improvements in time-on-task and skill proficiency. However, proactive tutoring, on average, showed marginally higher MAP growth (75%, p = .065) than reactive tutoring, i.e., proactive tutoring was more beneficial to students farther below the cutoff and helped narrow achievement gaps. Our findings provide evidence that differentiated human-AI tutoring addresses the needs of both groups, offering a practical and cost-effective strategy for scaling hybrid instruction.

Title: Inference on the Value of Policy Improvement in Adaptive Experiments
Authors: Justin Whitehouse, Emma Brunskill, Vasilis Syrgkanis
Affiliations: Stanford University
Abstract: In this paper, we develop an asymptotically normal estimator for the value of policy improvement (VPI) under adaptively collected data. This value, which is defined as the gap between the value of the best treatment policy in a class and that of a baseline policy, gauges whether or not it is worth deploying a personalized treatment policy. Building an estimator for the VPI is naturally more difficult than estimating the value of a fixed policy. This is because, in addition to contending with the correlated data and decaying propensities associated with adaptive experiments, any estimator must also handle the non-regularity, or lack of pathwise differentiability, of the underlying estimand when the optimal policy is non-unique. Our proposed estimator works by sequentially fitting a weighted empirical welfare maximizing policy on historical data and then evaluating it using inverse propensity weighting on future samples. We neither assume that the optimal policy is unique nor make a margin assumption on the underlying heterogeneous treatment effects. A key difficulty in analyzing our estimator is showing that the regret incurred through policy learning is asymptotically smaller than the standard error of the estimator. We accomplish this by showing faster regret rates for policy learning under decaying propensities, which may be of independent interest. We not only evaluate the coverage of our estimator on a mix of synthetic and semi-synthetic data, but also employ it to estimate the VPI in an adaptive experiment evaluating the efficacy of job assistance programs in Jordan due to Caria et al. Although our estimates are generally more conservative than their hierarchical Bayesian analysis, which assumes that the optimal policy is unique, we still corroborate the benefits of personalization amongst Syrian refugees.

Title: Instructor-designed AI improves learning in a randomized trial across 19 universities
Authors: Jun Li, Robert Bray, Sébastien Martin, Nils Van den Steen, Andrew Wu, Xiao Ni, Arielle Anderer, Ekaterina Astashkina, Владимир Бабич, Jean-Paul Baldwin, Hamsa Bastani, Christian Blanco, Oğuzhan Çelebi, Christopher Chen, Shi Chen, Benjamin C. Collier, Yao Cui, Pnina Feldman, Blair Flicker, Brian Han, Yichun Hu, Daniela Hurtado-Lange, Jane Jiang, Zhaohui Jiang, Ismail Kirci, Murat Köksalan, Zhen Lian, Hongyan Liang, Mengshi Lu, Lesley Meng, Ken Moon, Mi Kyong Newsom, Minje Park, Chris Parker, Anyan Qi, Meng Qi, Debjit Roy, Neha Sharma, Alp Sungu, Tom Tan, Necati Tereyağoğlu, Hanu Tyagi, Sriram Venkataraman, Guihua Wang, Yixin Wang, Owen Wu, Zonghao Yang, Qiuping Yu, Sophie Yu, Jingwei Zhang, Wenchang Zhang, Ruihao Zhu
Affiliations: Northwestern University; University of Michigan; Southern Methodist University; Cornell University
Abstract: Universities are alarmed by recent evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) can undermine learning, with students prescribed generic chatbots or centrally designed AI tools performing worse. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial across 7,200 students at 19 universities over three semesters, we tested whether AI designed by frontline instructors can improve learning. We encouraged instructors to design AI solutions they believed would best help their students. Drawing on their unique knowledge of their classes and students, the instructors created a wide array of innovations. We show that these instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning, measured by AI-proof assessments (proctored, in-person examinations). We found no change in student engagement, measured by course activity records, or satisfaction, measured by course evaluations. Our findings demonstrate that AI can improve student learning when its adoption is frontline-driven, with instructors empowered to design and refine AI solutions for their own classrooms.

Title: Joint Service Depth and Priority Design in Queueing Systems
Authors: Adam N. Elmachtoub, Yash Kanoria, Jonathan Y. Tan
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: In AI-assisted service systems, the server can choose how much processing effort to spend on each job, which we call the service depth. Deeper reasoning improves output quality but occupies the server longer and increases congestion, and the realized processing time remains random because AI models are probabilistic and tasks vary in complexity. We study the joint design of service depth and priority in a single-server queue whose customers differ in delay sensitivity, with the goal of maximizing social welfare. For each customer type, the decision maker chooses a priority level and a service depth, and service times are exponential with mean equal to the chosen depth. With two customer types and linear service values, we characterize the centralized optimum. Counterintuitively, it prioritizes the patient type and gives it a smaller service depth when patient customers are sufficiently prevalent. When delay sensitivity is private, however, incentive compatibility requires the impatient type to receive a weakly shorter sojourn time, so the optimal price menu never prioritizes the patient type. Consequently, there can be a welfare gap between the centralized decision maker's optimal control policy and the optimal decentralized pricing mechanism. With a continuum of types, the centralized optimum is monotone: more delay-sensitive customers receive weakly smaller depth and higher priority, so the optimum can be implemented by a price menu with no welfare loss. Allowing randomized depths similarly closes the gap in the two-type model. Finally, we calibrate an agentic AI service system using published coding-agent trials from DeepSWE and numerically examine priority inversion, the value of joint design, and the welfare gain from personalization.

Title: JustOPD: On-Policy Distillation from Autoregressive to Diffusion Language Models
Authors: Zikun Zhang, Jiayuan Sheng, David D. W. Yao, Wenpin Tang
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training approach for large language models (LLMs) that enables a student model to learn a teacher model's distribution from sequences sampled from the student's own policy. Despite its promising capability, OPD for diffusion language models (DLMs) remains underexplored and existing studies primarily focuses on DLM-to-DLM distillation. The limited availability of strong teacher DLMs and the flexible generation order of DLMs impose additional technical challenges as well. However, it remains unclear how to effectively distill knowledge from a strong autoregressive language model (ARM) into a weaker DLM, given the mismatch between the left-to-right decoding of ARMs and the flexible decoding order of DLMs. Inspired by Ni et al. (2026), we propose JustOPD, an ARM-to-DLM on-policy distillation method that uses autoregressive rollouts during training to align the student's generation process with the ARM teacher's left-to-right decoding. This alignment enables effective distillation from ARM teachers while preserving the DLM's flexible generation-order capability at inference time. Experiments using Qwen3-14B as the teacher and Dream-7B as the student demonstrate that JustOPD consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance over the base DLM across multiple divergence choices.

Title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
Authors: Yixiao Wang, Srikar Katta, Jon P. Donnelly, Emanuele Borgonovo, Cynthia D Rudin
Affiliations: Duke University; Johns Hopkins University; Bocconi University
Abstract: Computing local-level variable importance (VI) is critical for understanding machine learning models. Local permutation-based VI metrics offer a simple yet powerful approach, measuring how much a model's output changes when perturbing its inputs. However, existing perturbation strategies often ignore feature dependence or account for it only through restricted approximations. Perturbing a feature without fully respecting this dependence can generate unrealistic counterfactuals, thereby evaluating the model in regions unsupported by the observed data distribution. We address this gap by introducing a new model-agnostic local VI metric and estimator, Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with conditional Density estimation (LUCID). LUCID perturbs features of interest using plausible values drawn from the full conditional distribution given the remaining observed features. We establish theoretical connections between LUCID and existing VI measures, and provide an estimator with convergence guarantees and uncertainty quantification. Finally, we demonstrate LUCID's stable performance and practical utility across simulated and real-world examples.

Title: LagNet: Lag-Structured Operators for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
Authors: Zhenan Yu, Guangxin Jiang, Jiuyun Jiang, Jin Yang
Affiliations: Harbin Institute of Technology
Abstract: Long-term time series forecasting maps a finite history window to an extended future horizon. Many existing models focus primarily on the design of input representations and model structures, while paying less attention to the structural form of the history-to-future forecasting operator itself. We examine this operator directly and find that, across model families, sensitivity matrices exhibit recurring diagonal patterns whose diagonals correspond to relative temporal lags. Motivated by this observation, we develop a framework for direct multi-step forecasting based on lag-structured temporal operators. Its basic building block, LagLayer, constructs a Toeplitz matrix by tying history-to-future connections with the same relative lag and incorporates horizon-wise and history-wise scaling coefficients to relax exact sharing. This design enables LagLayer to serve as an effective replacement for temporal linear layers in existing forecasting models. Stacking LagLayer modules with activations and multiple feature maps yields LagNet. Experiments on long-term time series forecasting benchmarks show that our method is competitive with strong baselines, while sensitivity matrix diagnostics and limited-data experiments demonstrate that LagLayer provides an effective and sample-efficient alternative to a linear layer.

Title: Large-Scale Optimization Model Auto-Formulation: Harnessing LLM Flexibility via Structured Workflow
Authors: Kuo Liang, Yuhang Lu, Jianming Mao, Shuyi Amelia Sun, Chunwei Yang, Congcong Zeng, Xiao Jin, Hanzhang Qin, Ruihao Zhu, Chung-Piaw Teo
Affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; National University of Singapore; Shanghai University of Finance and Economics; City University of Hong Kong; Cornell University
Abstract: Large-scale optimization is a key backbone of modern business decision-making. However, building these models is often labor-intensive and time-consuming. We address this by proposing LEAN-LLM-OPT, a LightwEight AgeNtic workflow construction framework for LLM-assisted large-scale OPTimization auto-formulation. LEAN-LLM-OPT takes as input a problem description together with associated datasets and orchestrates a team of LLM agents to produce an optimization formulation. Specifically, upon receiving a query, two upstream LLM agents dynamically construct a workflow that specifies, step-by-step, how optimization models for similar problems can be formulated. A downstream LLM agent then follows this workflow to generate the final output. The agentic workflow leverages common modeling practices to structure the modeling process into a sequence of sub-tasks, offloading mechanical data-handling operations to auxiliary tools. This reduces the LLM's burden in planning and data handling, allowing us to exploit its flexibility to address unstructured components. Extensive simulations show that LEAN-LLM-OPT, instantiated with GPT-4.1 and the open source gpt-oss-20B, achieves strong performance on large-scale optimization modeling tasks and is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches. In addition, in a Singapore Airlines choice-based revenue management use case, LEAN-LLM-OPT demonstrates practical value by achieving leading performance across a range of scenarios. Along the way, we introduce Large-Scale-OR and Air-NRM, the first comprehensive benchmarks for large-scale optimization auto-formulation. The code and data of this work is available at https://github.com/CoraLiang01/lean-llm-opt.

Title: Learning Mixtures of Exponential Family
Authors: Mansi Sood, Devavrat Shah
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Motivated by causal inference and physical computing systems, we consider the problem of learning mixture of two bounded-support exponential-family distributions with a shared interaction parameter matrix and mixture component-specific linear parameter vectors. The unknown sequence of component labels belongs to a known structured class. We propose an estimator based on a convex loss that avoids the log-partition function; for each fixed label assignment, estimation is a convex optimization problem. We show that the conditional population loss uniquely identifies the interaction matrix and the linear parameter attached to each sample. For a global empirical minimizer, we establish finite-sample bounds on the interaction error in Frobenius norm and the average squared linear-parameter error. The bounds depend on the logarithm of the number of admissible label assignments, and, for fixed dimension and model bounds, imply consistency when this complexity grows sublinearly with sample size. Additional occupancy and separation conditions yield component and label recovery.

Title: Let's Have a Conversation: Designing and Evaluating LLM Agents for Interactive Optimization
Authors: Joshua Drossman, Alexandre Jacquillat, Sébastien Martin
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Northwestern University
Abstract: Optimization is as much about modeling the right problem as solving it. Identifying the right objectives, constraints, and trade-offs demands extensive interaction between researchers and stakeholders. Large language models can empower decision-makers with optimization capabilities through interactive optimization agents that can propose, interpret and refine solutions. However, it is fundamentally harder to evaluate a conversation-based interaction than traditional one-shot approaches. This paper proposes a scalable and replicable methodology for evaluating optimization agents through conversations. We build LLM-powered decision agents that role-play diverse stakeholders, each governed by an internal utility function but communicating like a real decision-maker. We generate thousands of conversations in a school scheduling case study. Results show that one-shot evaluation is severely limiting: the same optimization agent converges to much higher-quality solutions through conversations. Then, this paper uses this methodology to demonstrate that tailored optimization agents, endowed with domain-specific prompts and structured tools, can lead to significant improvements in solution quality in fewer interactions, as compared to general-purpose chatbots. These findings provide evidence of the benefits of emerging solutions at the AI-optimization interface to expand the reach of optimization technologies in practice. They also uncover the impact of operations research expertise to facilitate interactive deployments through the design of effective and reliable optimization agents.

Title: Logarithmic Regret for Alternating Mirror Descent
Authors: Tianlong Nan, Christian Kroer
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: Alternating online mirror descent (AltOMD) is a simple learning rule for zero-sum games, which improves upon simultaneous OMD numerically and theoretically. Previous work obtained $O(T^{1/3})$ and $O(T^{1/5})$ regret bounds for AltOMD, by leveraging modified-energy-function-based analyses. However, settling whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret has remained an open question. In this paper we resolve the question of whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret in the affirmative. In particular, we show an $O(log(T))$ regret bound on the sum of the players' external regrets for any two-player zero-sum bilinear game with compact convex strategy sets, under mild regularity assumptions on the regularizers. We verify that our assumptions hold for the negative entropy regularizer, thereby obtaining logarithmic regret for the alternating multiplicative weights updates algorithm. The regret bound also yields an $O(log(T)/T)$ duality gap bound for the averaged strategies.

Title: Match Rate Is Not Match Quality
Authors: Tobias Konitzer, David M. Rothschild
Abstract: Third-party identity-resolution vendors commonly emphasize match rate, the share of submitted records they can link to identifiers for advertising activation, as their core metric of quality. Yet a high match rate does not necessarily mean that those matched identifiers belong to the submitted records (i.e., the intended targets). In this paper we explore match quality as an alternative metric to match rate, utilizing a unique data set to evaluate match quality. We are able to compare two demographics, age and gender, from a submitted record (voter files) to the same demographics in self-reported surveys matched to mobile advertising identifiers linked together by two leading identity-resolution vendors. The data and matching was from 2019-20. There is substantial ambiguity in match quality of the returned records. First, both vendors' activation files contain multiple device identifiers per match. Second, match quality among audited pairs (Vendor A) and for explicitly labeled individual-level matches (Vendor B) is only 21.8% and 23.6%, respectively. Utilizing a mixture model that assumes that correct links always agree on these two demographics and incorrect links agree 10% of the time, these rates imply conditional identity-level precisions of approximately 15% and 13%, respectively. This paper utilizes identity-resolution products that are several years old, but the question we address remains fundamental: match rate alone cannot establish whether advertisers are reaching the people they intended. Evaluating identity resolution requires independent evidence of match quality alongside match rate.

Title: Measuring Where Intent Gets Lost in Agentic Smart Contract Synthesis
Authors: Abhinav Goel, Agostino Capponi, Alfio Gliozzo, Chaitya Shah
Affiliations: Columbia University; IBM (United States)
Abstract: AI agents can now write software from a plain-English description, but code that runs is not the same as code that does what was asked. This gap matters most for smart contracts, the programs behind Web3 applications that move money on a blockchain and cannot be fixed once deployed. We ask how to check whether an AI-written contract behaves as it should, and where the requested behavior gets lost. We design an evaluation built on execution rather than opinion. We replay the same transactions on an AI-written contract and on the original it should reproduce and measure how often they agree. We test every grading tool on planted mistakes, compare against an answer key written without the description, and audit our own scorer until known wrong answers cannot pass. Common methods, such as AI judges and standard analysis tools, miss obvious mistakes, and scoring choices matter too. Checking only the functions every system includes hid about half the difference between pipelines. We then propose an elicitation-first architecture. Before writing code, the agent asks the client a short checklist of questions, checks the contract against an independently written executable answer key, and returns disagreements to the client instead of silently rewriting code. Asking first matters far more than reviewing or patching afterwards, across three AI models, while automated security fixes often break requested behavior. A few well-chosen questions recover much of what a short description omits, and their value can be estimated without the original contract. To our knowledge, this is the first study in smart contract synthesis to gather missing requirements before generation and check the result against an independently written executable model. The lessons extend to any setting where AI agents turn requests into programs. We release our tools, 600 tasks and all results.

Title: MetaboLLM: a metabolomics-specialized large language model for biochemical knowledge integration and predictive metabolite graph construction
Authors: Dohyun Ku, Min Gu Kwak, Francisco J. Pasquel, Jing Li
Affiliations: Capital One (United States); Emory University; Georgia Institute of Technology
Abstract: Metabolomics knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous resources and remains difficult to translate into predictive representations. We developed MetaboLLM, a metabolomics-specialized large language model adapted through continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and structured retrieval, together with MetaboLLM-GIN, which converts generated biochemical descriptions into metabolite graphs for patient-level prediction using a graph isomorphism network. Across four backbone families, MetaboLLM outperformed corresponding base and medically adapted models on metabolomics knowledge, relational, and description tasks, and transferred to an external public benchmark. MetaboLLM-GIN achieved the highest AUC for stress hyperglycemia prediction after coronary artery bypass grafting (0.8616) and postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification (0.8123), outperforming conventional models, alternative graph constructions, and graphs generated from unadapted or non-retrieval LLM configurations. Model interpretation further produced biologically meaningful findings in both applications. These results show that domain-specialized language models can organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive and interpretable metabolite graph representations.

Title: Minimax Regret for Sobolev Kernel-Based Reinforcement Learning
Authors: Haichen Hu, David Simchi‐Levi
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: We study the minimax regret rate for episodic kernel-based reinforcement learning, where the expected reward and transition density belong to a Sobolev reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), with continuous state and action spaces, and adversarial initial states. For Sobolev smoothness parameter $ν>0$, state dimension $d_S$, and action dimension $d_A$, we prove that the minimax expected regret over $T$ episodes is $\widetildeΘ(T^{\max\{e_A,e_B\}})$, where $e_A=\frac{ν+d_A}{2ν+d_A}$, $e_B=\frac{ν+d_A+3d_S/2}{2ν+d_A+2d_S}$ with the other model parameters fixed. The two exponents reflect the distinct difficulties of action selection and learning across states. We introduce Sobolev Optimal Value Iteration (\texttt{SOVI}), which attains this rate from observed rewards and transitions. For fixed smoothness and reference-kernel lengthscale, its regret bound has a prefactor polynomial in the state-action dimension $d=d_S+d_A$, horizon $H$, reward and transition RKHS norm bounds $B_r,B_p$, and the norm-comparison factor $Λ$, up to logarithmic factors; $Λ=1$ for normalized Matérn kernels. The algorithm separates initial action selection from continuation-value estimation and combines local polynomial approximation with the shared RKHS structure of the approximation errors. Our matching upper and lower bounds determine the optimal dependence on the number of episodes for Sobolev kernel-based reinforcement learning regret minimization. Thus, we partially address the open problem in Vakili(2024) under Sobolev kernel RL.

Title: Minimax-Optimal Static Estimators Under Interference
Authors: Arthur Delarue, Ilan Lobel
Affiliations: University of Virginia; New York University
Abstract: We study the problem of estimating the global treatment effect in randomized experiments under interference, where a unit's outcome may depend on the treatment assignments of other units. We adopt a minimax framework, allowing an adversary to select an outcome function from a class of functions that satisfy bounded outcomes and bounded interference. We derive minimax-optimal static estimators that are robust to a wide range of interference structures, parameterized by a scalar $δ$ controlling the maximum influence of one unit's treatment on another's outcome. Under large interference, we observe two regimes. When the treatment and control groups are equally sized, the minimax-optimal static estimator is the zero estimator. When one of the two groups is larger, the minimax-optimal static estimator is a "half-zero" estimator, in which the outcomes of the smaller group are ignored, and the estimator only considers the outcomes of the larger group.

Title: Miscalibrated AI improves human calibration: An alignment problem for AI-assisted Decision education
Authors: Phillip Hegeman, Eeshan Hasan, Eungik Lee, Andrew Caplin, Jennifer S. Trueblood
Affiliations: Indiana University Bloomington; The Ohio State University; Federal Reserve Bank of New York; New York University
Abstract: Using artificial intelligence (AI) well requires probabilistic thinking, and central to it is calibration: expressing certainty that matches one's actual accuracy. Calibration is a decision skill, but a notoriously difficult one to teach. Because AI systems typically generate a probability alongside every prediction, observing these probabilities may help humans learn to provide better calibrated judgments. This is one form of what we call AI-assisted decision education -- using AI to teach the judgment skills that decision-making requires -- of which learning by observation, as here, is among the simplest forms. In a preregistered experiment, novice participants (N = 300) judged the probability that images of white blood cells were cancerous, before and after exposure to a highly accurate (94%) convolutional neural network. A single model was shown in three ways, holding accuracy fixed while varying the certainty it expressed: its original probabilities, which were conservative and poorly calibrated for the model's accuracy; a recalibrated version, well calibrated for the model and correspondingly certain; or categorical predictions carrying no probability information. When later tested without the AI, only the original, conservative display improved participants' calibration. It did so by reducing over-extremity, without a condition-specific improvement in discrimination. Notably, the display that taught best was the one miscalibrated for the model. AI-assisted decision education therefore faces an alignment problem: the signal that best describes a model, need not be the signal that best supports the learner.

Title: Moment Ambiguity and the Limits of Robust Stochastic Optimization
Authors: Andrés Cristi, Matteo Russo, J. Zhang
Abstract: We study fundamental information-theoretic limits of robust stochastic optimization when the distribution is known only through its exact moment sequence. We develop a unified framework that produces families of distinct distributions sharing all moments yet inducing radically different optimal decisions, thereby establishing strong impossibility results for a range of decision problems under moment ambiguity. Our binary and $N$-way moment-matching constructions separate quantiles, threshold regions, and online selection opportunities while preserving every moment. For the newsvendor problem, moment equivalence causes quantile ambiguity, inducing any fixed or randomized order quantity to fail arbitrarily badly. For revenue maximization, no deterministic or randomized posted pricing scheme can secure a nontrivial approximation relative to the full-information benchmark. For the secretary problem with cardinal observations, the optimal robust success probability under exact moment disclosure is the classical finite-horizon value $s_m$, even for i.i.d. observations. This value converges to $1/e$, compared with the full-information limit of approximately $0.5801$ due to Gilbert and Mosteller (J. Am. Stat. Assoc., 1966). We also recover and expand upon the recent impossibility result of Correa et al. (STOC, 2026) for prophet inequalities with moment knowledge. For every fixed $r\ge1$, exact moment knowledge can yield at best a $Θ(1/\log m)$ competitive ratio, even when competing against relaxed benchmarks based on expected $r$-th order statistics or when the algorithm is allowed to select $r$ items.

Title: Monetizing Intelligence: Advertising and Subscription Design on LLM Platforms
Authors: Yuhang Ji, Fasheng Xu, Tianjun Feng
Affiliations: Fudan University; University of Connecticut

Title: Monotonicity in streaming problems
Authors: Gustavo Bergantiños, Juan D. Moreno‐Ternero
Affiliations: Universidade de Vigo; Universidad Pablo de Olavide
Abstract: We explore the implications of the principle of monotonicity in the problem of sharing the revenues raised from subscriptions to music streaming platforms among content providers. We formalize various forms of this principle as several axioms for popularity indices, which generate sharing rules in this setting. We show that, combined with some other basic axioms (such as additivity, symmetry, or pairwise homogeneity), they provide axiomatic characterizations of focal indices for this problem, as well as more general families comprising them.

Title: Multistage Conditional Compositional Optimization
Authors: Buse Şen, Yifan Hu, Daniel Kühn
Affiliations: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey; École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne
Abstract: We introduce Multistage Conditional Compositional Optimization (MCCO) as a new paradigm for decision-making under uncertainty that combines aspects of multistage stochastic programming and conditional stochastic optimization. MCCO minimizes a nest of conditional expectations and nonlinear cost functions. It has numerous applications and arises, for example, in optimal stopping, linear-quadratic regulator problems, distributionally robust contextual bandits, as well as in problems involving dynamic risk measures. The naïve nested sampling approach for MCCO suffers from the curse of dimensionality familiar from scenario tree-based multistage stochastic programming, that is, its scenario complexity grows exponentially with the number of nests. We develop new multilevel Monte Carlo techniques for MCCO whose scenario complexity grows only polynomially with the desired accuracy.

Title: No Certificate, No Execution: Certified Traces as a Foundation for Trustworthy AI Agents
Authors: Xiao-Yang Liu Yanglet, Xiaodong Wang, Agostino Capponi
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: We argue that trustworthy AI agents, especially in high-stakes and policy-governed domains, should make execution conditional on certified traces rather than rely only on stronger generative models, output-level guardrails, or post-hoc audits. A generative agent may propose recommendations, tool calls, reports, or actions, but generation is not permission: an action may be computable yet impermissible, and individually permissible actions may compose into an impermissible trace. We formalize trustworthy agency through a \textbf{Proposal--Certification--Execution (PCE)} architecture: a probabilistic generating machine $M_G$ proposes candidate execution traces, a \textbf{Permissibility Machine} $M_Π$ certifies proposed traces under a policy system $Π$, and execution proceeds only for certified traces. The executable trace language is $L_{\mathrm{exec}} = L_G \cap L_{\mathrm{cert}}(M_Π)$. Before execution, a trace is a structured pre-execution record submitted for certification: it specifies intended steps, evidence, proposed tool calls, approvals, replayable computations, credentials, and execution conditions. This perspective complements chain-of-thought monitorability: visible reasoning may help detect misbehavior, but monitorability is not certifiability, and reasoning is only one component of a broader execution trace. The formal principle is simple: an agent-generated trace should execute only when it carries a checkable certificate witnessing permissibility under $Π$: \textbf{no certificate, no execution}. We develop certified traces and Permissibility Machines as foundations for trustworthy AI agents, connect trace certification to proof-carrying execution, proof memory, privacy, and zero-knowledge certificates, and propose evaluating agents by what generated traces can be safely certified for execution, not by output accuracy alone.

Title: Nonparametric GARCH: An Iterated Neural Estimator
Authors: Guohao Shen, Ngai Hang Chan, Ruizhi Deng
Affiliations: Hong Kong Polytechnic University; City University of Hong Kong

Title: Not All LPs Are Equal: The Active-Passive Gap in Automated Market Maker Liquidity Provision
Authors: Agathe Sadeghi, Dingyue Liu, Ciamac C. Moallemi, Xin Wan, Brian Zhu
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: Liquidity provision in automated market makers is typically analyzed at the pool level, implicitly assuming LP homogeneity. This aggregate view can hide how liquidity provision outcomes differ between LP strategies, particularly as concentrated liquidity AMM designs operating on high-performance blockchains allow liquidity to be actively repositioned around trades. We develop a markout-based framework to decompose Uniswap LP profitability into active and passive components using two complementary methods: a LIFO subtraction method that matches short-lived mint-burn positions and attributes swap-level markouts by liquidity share; and an infinitesimal LP benchmark that estimates the performance of a fully passive, always-in-range marginal LP directly from the AMM price path. We apply these methods to Uniswap v2, v3, and v4 pools on Ethereum, Arbitrum, and Base chains, and find passive profitability can materially differ from aggregate pool profitability. In Uniswap v2, with liquidity distributed evenly and active LP behavior nearly absent, the overall and passive markouts are almost the same. In contrast, concentrated-liquidity pools have a systematic active-passive gap: passive LPs tend to underperform aggregate pool-level measures. The gap is wider on Ethereum than on L2s, consistent with active liquidity provision being more useful when block times and ordering conditions allow LPs to react to incoming flow. In general, passive LPs perform better on higher fee pools. The LIFO and infinitesimal estimates are generally consistent directionally across most pools, providing evidence of the robustness of the decomposition. The results suggest that adverse selection in AMMs is not evenly distributed among LPs, with important implications for LP strategy, fee-tier design and measurement of DEX market quality.

Title: OBLIQ-Bench: Exposing Overlooked Bottlenecks in Modern Retrievers with Latent and Implicit Queries
Authors: Diane Tchuindjo, Devavrat Shah, Omar Khattab
Abstract: Retrieval benchmarks are increasingly saturating, but we argue that efficient search is far from a solved problem. We identify a class of queries we call oblique, which seek documents that instantiate a latent pattern, like finding all tweets that express an implicit stance, chat logs that demonstrate a particular failure mode, or transcripts that match an abstract scenario. We study three mechanisms through which obliqueness may arise and introduce OBLIQ-Bench, a suite of five oblique search problems over real long-tail corpora. OBLIQ-Bench exposes an overlooked asymmetry between retrieval and verification, where reasoning LLMs reliably recognize latent relevance whenever relevant documents are surfaced, but even sophisticated retrieval pipelines fail to surface most relevant documents in the first place. We hope that OBLIQ-Bench will drive research into retrieval architectures that efficiently capture latent patterns and implicit signals in large corpora.

Title: Oblivious Learning and Collusive Pricing
Authors: Yuhang Wu, Assaf J. Zeevi
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: On a platform with many sellers, should a pricing algorithm explicitly model competitors' prices when learning demand? Classical arguments suggest that ignoring competitors induces model misspecification and inefficiency, yet findings from algorithmic collusion suggest that ignoring competitor prices may, surprisingly, facilitate collusive outcomes and improve profits. We study this problem in a competitive market with unknown noisy demand, in which sellers repeatedly set prices, either incorporating competitor prices in learning their demand models (informed), or ignoring them (oblivious). We show that, relative to a monopolist, an oblivious seller in a competitive market must conduct more aggressive price exploration to compensate for the loss of dynamic competitor information. When all sellers are oblivious, prices converge to the competitive outcome under persistent exploration, while a continuum of pseudo-equilibria arises when exploration is "insufficient." In markets with a mix of oblivious and informed sellers, the informed strictly out-earn the oblivious. In game-theoretic terms, the unique Nash equilibrium is the all-informed market, in which prices converge to the competitive outcome efficiently, and oblivious modeling does not robustly lead to collusive patterns.

Title: Observing the unobserved confounding through its effects: toward randomized trial-like estimates from real-world survival data
Authors: Vasiliki Stoumpou, Dimitris Bertsimas, Samuel Singer, Georgios Antonios Margonis
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
Abstract: Background: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are costly, time-consuming, and often infeasible, while treatment-effect estimation from observational data is limited by unobserved confounding. Methods: We developed a three-step framework to address unobserved confounding in observational survival data. First, we infer a latent prognostic factor (U) from restricted mean survival time (RMST) discrepancies between patients with similar observed factors, the same treatment, and divergent outcomes, leveraging the idea that the aggregate effect of unmeasured factors can be inferred even if individual factors cannot. Second, we balance U with observed baseline covariates using prognostic matching, entropy balancing, or inverse probability of treatment weighting. Third, we apply multivariable survival analysis to estimate hazard ratios (HRs). We evaluated the framework in three observational cohorts with RCT benchmarks, two RCT cohorts, and six multicenter observational cohorts. Results: In three observational cohorts (nine comparisons), balancing U improved agreement with trial HRs in all cases; in the strongest settings, it reduced absolute log-HR error by approximately ten-fold versus using observed covariates alone (mean reduction 0.344; p=0.001). In two RCT cohorts, U was balanced across arms (most SMDs <0.1) and adjustment had minimal impact on log-HRs (mean absolute change 0.08). Across six multicenter cohorts, balancing U within centers reduced cross-center dispersion in chemotherapy log-HR estimates (mean reduction 0.147; p=0.016); when populations were directly balanced across centers to account for case-mix differences, cross-center survival differences were narrowed in 75%-100% of comparisons. Conclusions: Inferring and balancing a latent prognostic signal may reduce unobserved confounding and improve treatment-effect estimation from real-world data.

Title: On Competing Sellers with Substitutable Goods
Authors: Moshe Babaioff, Yuval Grofman, Brendan Lucier, Raghuvansh R. Saxena
Affiliations: Hebrew University of Jerusalem; Microsoft Research New England (United States); Tata Institute of Fundamental Research
Abstract: We study mechanism design by an incumbent seller facing competition from an entrant seller of a substitute good. The incumbent commits to a potentially randomized mechanism before her competitor responds. A unit-demand buyer with fixed, publicly known values for the two goods observes both mechanisms and may interact with them in either order. How should a revenue-maximizing incumbent design her mechanism when her product is superior or inferior to her competitor's? We determine the incumbent's exact optimal revenue and characterize all mechanisms that obtain it. Commitment and randomization allow her to earn strictly positive revenue even against an arbitrarily superior product, despite earning nothing under posted-price (i.e., Bertrand) competition. Optimal mechanisms can require a continuum of lottery options, even though the buyer selects only one in equilibrium: unselected options shape the competitor's incentives rather than screen private buyer information. We also show that the buyer's ability to choose the interaction order can be strictly beneficial to the incumbent, even though the incumbent is always visited first at equilibrium. Finally, we show that without commitment, every pure Nash equilibrium yields Bertrand revenues even with randomized mechanisms.

Title: On the convergence of doubly stochastic Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient Method
Authors: Yiheng Xiao, Huikang Liu
Affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract: We study a block-structured class of convex-concave saddle-point problems in which both the primal and dual variables admit natural separable decompositions. Motivated by large-scale applications where a full update on either side can be computationally expensive, we propose a doubly stochastic primal--dual hybrid gradient method (DSPDHG) that performs randomized block updates on both primal and dual variables.The method extends classical PDHG and stochastic PDHG (SPDHG) schemes in a unified manner:it reduces to deterministic PDHG when all blocks are selected and to one-sided stochastic variants when only one side is randomized. For the general convex setting, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(1/K)$ ergodic convergence rate for the expected restricted primal--dual gap under suitable blockwise step-size conditions. We further analyze a restarted variant of DSPDHG under a quadratic growth condition in terms of the smoothed primal-dual gap. Under this regularity assumption, we prove linear convergence of the restarted outer iterates. Numerical evidence is provided to show that restarted DSPDHG with standard step sizes demonstrates competitive practical performance compared with PDHG, SPDHG, and their restarted variants.

Title: On-Trip Matching and Pricing for Shared Rides
Authors: Yifan Shen, Junlin Chen, Julia Yan, Chiwei Yan
Affiliations: University of Washington; Tsinghua University; University of British Columbia; University of California, Berkeley
Abstract: Shared rides, which match compatible riders in one vehicle, have the potential to increase vehicle utilization and reduce congestion and emissions. However, this service has seen limited success outside dense urban areas due to insufficient matching opportunities. The dominant model in the literature, which we refer to as the pre-trip model, matches riders before dispatch using non-bipartite matching, and dispatches unmatched riders solo. In practice, augmenting this pre-trip matching mechanism with an on-trip matching phase, where riders initially dispatched solo can still match with later arrivals, can expand matching opportunities. Yet the addition of the on-trip phase complicates the dynamic matching problem, as riders' matching opportunities evolve as they travel: both the set of compatible riders and the value of matches can diminish as a rider progresses towards her destination. To address this challenge, we formulate a Markov decision process that tracks riders' evolving states and weighs immediate matches against future matching opportunities. Within this framework, we incorporate pricing decisions to maximize long-run average profit, where we develop a fluid relaxation for static pricing and use value function approximation for dynamic (state-dependent) pricing. Experiments using Chicago ridesharing data show that pre-trip matching performs well with concentrated demand, whereas on-trip matching is particularly beneficial in the sparse outskirts where operating shared rides is especially challenging. Across both static and dynamic pricing settings, adding on-trip matching increases platform profit and match rates while lowering average quoted prices, showing the value of capturing matching opportunities along the route when demand is too dispersed for effective pre-trip matching.

Title: Online Generalized-Mean Welfare Maximization: Achieving Near-Optimal Regret from Samples
Authors: Zongjun Yang, Rachitesh Kumar, Christian Kroer
Affiliations: Columbia University; Carnegie Mellon University
Abstract: We study online fair allocation of $T$ sequentially arriving items among $n$ agents with heterogeneous preferences, with the objective of maximizing generalized-mean welfare, defined as the $p$-mean of agents' time-averaged utilities, with $p\in (-\infty, 1)$. We first consider the i.i.d. arrival model and show that the pure greedy algorithm -- which myopically chooses the welfare-maximizing integral allocation -- achieves $\widetilde{O}(1/T)$ average regret. Importantly, in contrast to prior work, our algorithm does not require distributional knowledge and achieves the optimal regret rate using only the online samples. We then go beyond i.i.d. arrivals and investigate a nonstationary model with time-varying independent distributions. In the absence of additional data about the distributions, it is known that every online algorithm must suffer $Ω(1)$ average regret. We show that only a single historical sample from each distribution is sufficient to recover the optimal $\widetilde{O}(1/T)$ average regret rate, even in the face of arbitrary non-stationarity. Our algorithms are based on the re-solving paradigm: they assume that the remaining items will be the ones seen historically in those periods and solve the resulting welfare-maximization problem to determine the decision in every period. Finally, we also account for distribution shifts that may distort the fidelity of historical samples and show that the performance of our re-solving algorithms is robust to such shifts.

Title: Online LLM Personalization from Pairwise Preferences Across Users
Authors: Romain Puech, Georgy Salakhutdinov, Dimitris Bertsimas
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Large language models can answer the same question in different styles, but users' preferred styles are hidden and vary across users and questions. We study inference-time personalization through online selection from a fixed set of prompts, each representing a persona. Users arrive sequentially, each asks a short sequence of questions, and the system displays two responses per question and observes one pairwise choice. We formulate this interaction as a variant of the contextual dueling bandit problem in which the learner starts without preference data, adapts within each session, and exploits information shared across users. The objective is to minimize cumulative strong regret, summing the utility gaps of both displayed responses relative to the user's best response among the available options. We make two contributions. First, we introduce the problem and release a reproducible preference benchmark and dataset built around a tutoring case study, containing educational questions, LLM-generated answers in six teaching styles, and pairwise judgments from LLM-simulated students with hidden preference profiles. We fit Bradley-Terry models to these judgments to obtain reference utilities for regret evaluation. Second, we propose a baseline that learns a mixture prior over users from completed sessions and adapts to each new user within the session. On students and topics never used in development, it removes 44-48% of random pairs' excess regret and achieves over half the performance of a per-user linear oracle fitted in hindsight. We release code, prompts, and the benchmark.

Title: Optimal Control of a Non-Stationary Inventory-Queue, with Applications to EV-Battery Swapping
Authors: Hanyu Cheng, David D. W. Yao
Affiliations: Tsinghua University; Columbia University
Abstract: We study a non-stationary queueing system with multiple parallel servers and a finite buffer capacity, over a finite planning horizon. Motivated by an operation that is central to an EV (electric vehicle) battery-swapping station -- how to best manage the charging of batteries swapped off from EVs, we develop a continuous-time MDP (Markov decision process) approach to the problem. The main technical challenge is to allow both the arrival rate and the service-cost rate to be functions of time with jumps at discrete time points, key features of the EV swapping station's operation. We derive an exact and explicit threshold structure that characterizes the optimal control policy. Moreover, we give conditions under which the thresholds are monotone over time, and with respect to key system parameters such as service and buffer capacities. Extensive numerical experiments are carried out to supplement as well as validate the theoretical results, and also to illustrate the robustness of the threshold structure in practical implementations.

Title: Optimal Learning in Fairness-Aware Contextual Bandits
Authors: Gengyu Xue, Fan Wang, Feiyu Jiang, Zifeng Zhao, Yi Yu
Affiliations: University of Warwick; The University of Melbourne; Fudan University; University of Notre Dame
Abstract: Mitigating unfair disparities in sequential decision-making is a growing concern in machine learning. We study contextual bandits under a global covariate-based Lipschitz fairness constraint, pioneered by \cite{dwork2012fairness}, requiring individuals with similar contexts to receive similar action distributions. We show that this constraint induces a randomisation region near the decision boundary and explicitly quantify the population level cost of fairness. We further establish a canonical representation of the optimal fair policy, which reduces the fair policy design to a lower-dimensional boundary optimisation problem. We develop a lazy fair greedy algorithm that exploits fairness-induced covariate diversity under continuous contexts, with policy updates computed via finite-dimensional linear programming. For general context distributions, including discrete and mixed contexts, we propose a lazy polyhedral upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm, whose optimistic optimisation reduces to finitely many linear programs over confidence-set vertices. Both methods satisfy fairness at every round and achieve regret of order $O(\sqrt{T} + T^{(d-2)/(d-1)}{\indc\{d\geq 4\}})$ up to poly-logarithmic factors, where $d$ is the dimension of the contexts. A matching minimax lower bound for $\ell_1$-based fairness establishes optimality, and reveals an unavoidable nonparametric cost of learning the decision boundary, which dominates the parametric learning cost when $d \geq 4$. Experiments on synthetic and real data support our theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our methods.

Title: Optimal Value Inference for Reinforcement Learning
Authors: Nan Lu, Ethan Lee, Ruicheng Ao, David Simchi‐Levi, Junwei Lu
Abstract: We study offline inference for the optimal value in reinforcement learning under finite state and action spaces. Two new nuisances are derived as fixed points of a self-induced Bellman equation, in which we approximate the maximum Bellman operator by its softmax correspondence. We propose a debiased estimator through the Neyman orthogonality and establish its asymptotic normality under diverging horizons even when the behavior policy changes with time, as long as the nuisances have the statistical rates that can be achieved by many machine learning methods. We provide a concrete estimating procedure for these nuisances and show they can lead to valid inference. Synthetic experiments validate the numerical performance of our inference method, and we implement it in real-life decision-making problems, including bike repositioning and AI agentic tool use.

Title: Optimality of Affine Policies in Distributionally Robust Linear-Quadratic Control with Temporally Correlated Noise
Authors: Jakob Nylöf, Daniel Kühn, John Lygeros, Giancarlo Ferrari-Trecate
Affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne; ETH Zurich
Abstract: We study finite-horizon distributionally robust linear-quadratic control with disturbances that can be arbitrarily correlated in time. The ambiguity set is modeled as a single 2-Wasserstein ball centered at a nominal elliptically contoured distribution of the disturbances. Despite the infinite-dimensionality of both the policy space and ambiguity set, we prove that the optimal policy is affine and that the worst-case distribution is an affine push-forward of the nominal distribution. These affine maps can be computed efficiently via a best-response algorithm based on the Frank--Wolfe algorithm. Experiments demonstrate improved out-of-sample performance over LQG and its distributionally robust extensions when the true disturbances are correlated, incurring only a small loss of performance under uncorrelated disturbances.

Title: Optimizing for Fairness in Generalized Kidney Exchange: Theory and Computations
Authors: Claire Chang, Arin Khare, David B. Shmoys
Affiliations: Cornell University
Abstract: The seminal work of Roth, Sönmez, & Ünver shows that the Edmonds-Gallai structure theorem for non-bipartite matching can be leveraged to yield a randomized algorithm to match patient-donor pairs in kidney exchange with extraordinarily strong properties. This breakthrough led to randomized polynomial-time algorithms to find a maximum-cardinality matching maximizing individual fairness objectives--measured by the probability that nodes are matched--such as Nash social welfare. But the exchanges allowed in practice go beyond cardinality matching, generalizing to weighted variants and allowing structures such as paths and 3-cycles. We show that strongly polynomial algorithms guaranteeing the same fairness properties can be obtained in weighted settings for matching and 2-paths. While even maximum cardinality coverage with cycles and paths of length at least three is NP-hard, we provide a general result showing that any optimization subroutine (for whichever structure is allowed) can be bootstrapped using a polynomial number of calls to yield a mechanism that has analogous fairness properties to those obtained for matching. We complement these theoretical results with computational results, both on well-studied synthetic data-sets and on samples drawn from real data, that demonstrate the striking advantages of adding fairness considerations to more general kidney-exchange mechanisms.

Title: Overlapping Reserves without a Common Priority: Theory and an Application to School Choice in Chile
Authors: Battal Doğan, Kenzo Imamura, M. Bumin Yenmez
Affiliations: University of Bristol
Abstract: We study matching markets with overlapping reserves governed by heterogeneous priorities. When applicants qualify for multiple reserves, how they are routed can affect reserve utilization and which applicants are admitted. We introduce classify-and-rank choice rules that yield strategy-proof deferred acceptance mechanisms satisfying maximum reserve utilization and priority-respect. We axiomatically characterize our mechanism's admission outcomes for any given classification and reserve order. With two reserve categories, we provide a foundation for the reserve order and establish its distributional implications for access across eligibility groups. Using nine cycles of Chilean school admissions, which feature such reserves, we document reserve-utilization failures under the deployed mechanism and show that their frequency depends sharply on the reserve order. We show how our mechanism can be adapted to Chile's institutional setting to prevent such failures. Under this alternative mechanism, the reserve order generates a distributional pattern across eligibility groups, consistent with our theory.

Title: Pathwise-Budgeted LLM Routing: Online Allocation with K-Bit Tail-Cost Learning
Authors: Hanzhang Qin, Sophie H. Yu, Yuewei Zhang, Zhihai Zhang
Affiliations: National University of Singapore
Abstract: Firms using large language models under fixed budgets must decide which model to call and whether to retry a failed task. Because a call's charge is revealed only after completion, one long response can exhaust the remaining budget and leave later tasks unserved. Our objective is to maximize the number of tasks solved before service stops. We develop a contextual bandit policy, ADP-HT, which learns each model's task-specific success probability and constructs conservative cost estimates from coarsened response-length labels on a quantile grid with $2^K$ intervals. The policy weighs predicted success against these costs, adjusting the cost penalty to realized spending and the budget available per remaining task. Under calibration, local regularity, and grid-coverage conditions, we bound the excess allowance in the policy's conservative cost estimates. At a fixed sample size, increasing $K$ reduces the discretization term but increases the estimation allowance. At the tightest tested budgets, ADP-HT solves more than twice as many MATH500 and GPQA tasks as the best implemented baseline. It achieves the highest mean cumulative score at ten of fourteen RouterBench budgets. On LiveCodeBench, it outperforms a deployed commercial router in both default and cost-saving modes at the three lowest test budgets.

Title: Paying for Information, Not for Clicks: A Block-Level Publisher Content Marketplace for AI Answers
Authors: Markus Möbius, Luca Braghieri, Sarah Eichmeyer, Daniel G. Goldstein, Nicole Immorlica, Olivér Kiss, Roee Levy, Brendan Lucier, Ishan Mahajan, Jingyi Qiu, Tanya Rosenblat, David M. Rothschild, András SÁRI, Alexsandrs Slivkins, Colin Watson
Affiliations: Microsoft (United States); Bocconi University; Tel Aviv University; University of Michigan; Central European University
Abstract: We propose a publisher content marketplace that allocates payments for information used in AI-generated answers. The unit of attribution is a ``lego block:'' a distinct fact or piece of commentary that may appear in articles from multiple publishers. A simple news-reading model connects three payment rules: equal sharing among all publishers reporting on a block, rewarding the publisher who reported a block first, and rewarding indispensable contributions. Each can be represented within a Shapley-value framework. We evaluate the framework using answers to 1,974 search-engine queries about a heavily covered news episode. When attribution considers only the articles retrieved for an individual query, most cited blocks appear unique, and the rules produce nearly identical allocations. A global index covering the full news corpus reveals overlap across publishers, making the choice of payment rule consequential. Premium publishers, defined as established outlets with substantial newsgathering operations, receive 42% of allocated value under equal sharing, compared with 46-50% under a first-publication rule, depending on the treatment of publication timestamps. These findings highlight the importance of a shared global index that records which publishers provide each block and when they published it. Attribution restricted to the sources retrieved for an individual answer lacks the information needed to distinguish these payment policies.

Title: Planetary Geospatial Foundation Models: A New Paradigm for Global Public Health
Authors: Arbaaz Muslim, Aviv Slobodkin, Katherine Wheeler-Martin, Eric Zhou, John Brittain, Martin Gerbert Frasch, Hamsa Subramaniam, Jacob Bien, Hamed Sadeghi, Sarah Conderino, Stone Jiang, Ben R. Spoer, Daniel Neill, Mimi Sun, Joydeep Paul, Yun Liu, Tomer Shekel, Amy Chung-Yu Chou, Anna Carter, Charles Elliott, Aaron Bell, Reuven Sayag, Avinatan Hassidim, Niv Efron, Yossi Matias, Kasumi Widner, Eduardo Lopez Ortiz, José Alberto Díaz-Quiñonez, Moritz U. G. Kraemer, John S. Brownstein, Isaias Fernandes Co, Etien Luc Koua, Monica Bharel, Benjamin M. Rader, Lorna Thorpe, Marc Gourevitch, Shravya Shetty, Gautam Prasad
Affiliations: NYU Langone Health; Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México; Secretaria de Salud; Boston Children's Hospital; World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa; Google (United States)
Abstract: The efficacy of traditional disease prediction is limited by spatial gaps and temporal lags, which impact the timing and targets of resource deployments. Outbreaks escalate undetected, chronic disease burdens are quantified years later, and at-risk populations in data-sparse regions remain unaddressed. Planetary geospatial foundation models complement existing epidemiological workflows to provide operational improvements, encoding multimodal search, mobility, and environmental signals into generalizable place representations. As illustrations of this complementarity, we present independent global health case studies of Google Earth AI's Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM) -- a foundation model for geospatial inference -- across four domains (vaccine-preventable, communicable, noncommunicable, maternal mental health), five tasks (spatial extrapolation, interpolation/nowcasting, probabilistic forecasting, prospective forecasting, risk stratification), and four countries (USA, Canada, Mexico, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo). Across these case studies, PDFM addresses critical surveillance gaps across domains: improving US-Canada border MMR vaccination coverage predictions by capturing cross-border behavioral spillovers domestic models miss; nowcasting cardiovascular disease to accelerate data availability; enhancing short-term municipal Mexican dengue forecasts for timely outbreak vector control; improving forecasts of cholera hotspots; and adding a transferable signal to individual-level postpartum-depression risk prediction in US states the model had never seen, while not replacing individual socioeconomic data or closing demographic screening gaps. Together, these results showcase capabilities of geospatial foundation models for public health surveillance.

Title: Platform architecture determines whether recommendation algorithms can shape information quality on social media
Authors: Mohammad Hammas Saeed, David André Broniatowski, Joseph R. Simons, Erica Lynn Gralla, Manan Suri, Giovanni Luca Ciampaglia
Affiliations: George Washington University; University of Maryland, College Park
Abstract: Social media platforms shape public discourse through two fundamental design choices that naturally co-occur in any field investigation: platform architecture, which defines what types of actors exist and how they interact, and recommendation algorithm, which determines what content is surfaced to users. Using agent-based simulation, we orthogonally manipulate both factors, exploring four prototypical architectures -- tree (e.g., Reddit), layered hierarchy (e.g., Facebook), network (e.g., Twitter), and complete graph (e.g., TikTok) -- and two algorithms: chronological (LIFO) and popularity-based (Hot). Drawing on prior theory that identifies and ranks canonical system architectures in terms of their flexibility we hypothesize that algorithmic effects on information spread and quality should be largest on the most flexible platforms and smallest on the most constrained ones. We find strong confirmation of this prediction. On tree-like platforms like Reddit, the algorithm has no detectable effect on information spread and quality. On layered hierarchies and networks like Facebook and Twitter, respectively, the Hot algorithm has modest positive effects on both the spread of information and its quality. On complete structures like TikTok, the Hot algorithm leads to a winner-take-all dynamics that has strong negative effects on both information spread and quality, making the relation between content quality and popularity unpredictable. These findings imply that architectural considerations are more powerful levers than algorithmic interventions for the design of healthy online spaces and public discourse. Platform reform efforts focused exclusively on algorithm choice may be insufficient on architecturally unconstrained platforms and unnecessary on architecturally constrained ones.

Title: Predictive and Prescriptive AI toward Optimizing Wildfire Suppression
Authors: Léonard Boussioux, Alexandre Jacquillat, Ryne Reger, Jacob Wachspress
Affiliations: University of Washington; Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Intense wildfire seasons require critical prioritization decisions to allocate scarce suppression resources over a dispersed geographical area. This paper develops a predictive and prescriptive approach to jointly optimize crew assignments and wildfire suppression. The problem features a discrete resource-allocation structure with endogenous wildfire demand and non-linear wildfire dynamics. We formulate an integer optimization model with crew assignments on a time-space-rest network, wildfire dynamics on a time-state network, and linking constraints between them. We develop a two-sided branch-and-price-and-cut algorithm based on: (i) a two-sided column generation scheme that generates fire suppression plans and crew routes iteratively; (ii) a new family of cuts exploiting the knapsack structure of the linking constraints; and (iii) novel branching rules to accommodate non-linear wildfire dynamics. We also propose a data-driven double machine learning approach to estimate wildfire spread as a function of covariate information and suppression efforts, mitigating observed confounding between historical crew assignments and wildfire growth. Extensive computational experiments show that the optimization algorithm scales to otherwise intractable real-world instances; and that the methodology can enhance suppression effectiveness in practice, resulting in significant reductions in area burned over a wildfire season and guiding resource sharing across wildfire jurisdictions.

Title: Preventing Model Extraction in Contextual Linear Optimization
Authors: Adam N. Elmachtoub, Tianyi Lin, Wenxuan Liu
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: Consider a contextual linear optimization problem, where a predict-then-optimize (PTO) system returns optimal decisions without revealing the cost vectors used in its downstream linear program. Our focus is on how to prevent attackers, who can submit context queries, from extracting the underlying prediction model. Although the cost-to-decision map is many-to-one, observations across contexts can reveal the underlying prediction model. For linear models, we provide sufficient conditions where the attacker can learn the model up to positive scaling by only observing the decision. These conditions motivate an adaptive attack that alternates inverse optimization with boundary sampling, i.e., using context queries leading to decision boundaries of the current attacker model. To prevent extraction, we propose a mechanism that perturbs decisions only when the predicted cost vector is near a decision boundary. We establish a regret bound in terms of the perturbation radius. For the attackers that fit the defended responses as optimal decisions under the evaluation distribution, we also prove a lower bound on expected extraction error. Experiments on synthetic instances and real data quantify the security-performance trade-off of the defense mechanism and illustrate that our defense can increase the extraction error.

Title: Primer: An AI Framework for Instructor-Centered Educational Simulation Creation
