Authors: Ethan Mollick, Lilach Mollick, Ben Przystanski, LJ Ciccarelli, Natalie Bach, Laura Zarrow
Affiliations: University of Pennsylvania

Title: Proportionality in Ranking Compression
Authors: Daniel Halpern, Xinyu Liu, Evi Micha, Yu Peng Ng, Warut Suksompong
Affiliations: Google (United States); University of Southern California; National University of Singapore
Abstract: Motivated by applications in reinforcement learning from human feedback, we consider a setting where a given collection of rankings needs to be compressed into a smaller collection of rankings. This can also be seen as a combination of two fundamental social choice frameworks: ranking aggregation and multiwinner voting. We propose three proportionality notions that capture different types of representation in this setting: positional proportionality, pairwise proportionality, and proportionality for solid coalitions (PSC). On the one hand, we show that positional proportionality and PSC are always satisfiable for any input rankings and target compression size, and a desired output can be found in polynomial time. On the other hand, we prove that pairwise proportionality cannot be satisfied in general, but can nevertheless be attained when the input rankings are single-peaked or single-crossing.

Title: PyVesta: A new Versatile Echelle Spectra exTraction and Analysis pipeline
Authors: Lukas Stock, Andreas Schrimpf
Affiliations: Philipps University of Marburg
Abstract: We present PyVesta, an automatic data reduction software for fiber fed echelle spectrographs. PyVesta is designed to be used with different instruments, both high resolution spectrographs such as HARPS or FEROS as well as inexpensive off-the-shelf spectrographs like the Shelyak eShel II. Special additions were implemented to improve the stability and resolution of inexpensive instruments especially. PyVesta provides tools for all extraction steps from raw CCD images to continuum normalized spectra, e.g., CCD image corrections, spectra extraction, wavelength calibration, and continuum normalization. Our software is based on the software package CERES and was ported to Python 3, revised, and supplemented.

Title: RAEM: Robust Autonomous Exploration for Multi-Floor Environments with a Quadruped Robot
Authors: Zikang Yuan, Yuan Ren, Yian Wang, Yixue Wang, Enze Fang, Xuewei Zhang, Junda Cheng, Chi Chen, Chin Pang Ho, Lijun Zhu, Shaohang Xu, Kwang-Ting Tim Cheng, Xin Yang
Affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; Southeast University; City University of Hong Kong; Huazhong University of Science and Technology; University of Hong Kong
Abstract: In this paper, we propose RAEM, a robust autonomous exploration framework for quadruped robots operating in multi-floor environments. Most existing ground-robot exploration approaches rely on planar traversability representations, which cannot adequately represent the overlapping structures and cross-floor connectivity of multi-floor buildings. Although tomography-based representations provide effective traversability modeling for multi-floor navigation, maintaining a global tomography map incurs substantial computational overhead for online exploration with frequent replanning. Moreover, sparse and fragmented LiDAR observations in stairwells can degrade local traversability estimation, leading to irregular viewpoint placement and temporary topological disconnections. To address these challenges, RAEM adopts a hybrid local-global traversability representation, in which a local tomography map and an explicitly categorized local 3D grid map are used for online terrain analysis and connectivity evaluation, while an elevation-aware global topological graph is incrementally constructed from these local spatial representations for efficient cross-floor exploration planning. We further introduce a staircase center alignment strategy to reduce abrupt yaw variations during climbing and a dual path searching mechanism to recover guidance paths when the global topology is locally disconnected. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate robust and computationally stable autonomous exploration across multi-floor structures, including continuous exploration of a five-floor stairwell.

Title: Reduced Cost Influence Functions for Predict-then-Optimize under Noisy Data
Authors: William Zhang, Saurabh Amin, Georgia Perakis
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Machine learning models deployed in decision-making pipelines, from vehicle routing to dynamic pricing to clinical decision support, must remain reliable in the face of low-quality training data. We study a predict-then-optimize setting in which an upstream model predicts the cost vector of a downstream linear program, with a large pool of noisy training data supplemented by a small curated set of clean data. We introduce Reduced Cost Influence Functions (RCIFs), which combine influence functions from robust statistics with the geometry of linear optimization to estimate how each training point shifts downstream decisions. Building on this, we propose a reweighting algorithm that uses RCIFs to downweight harmful training points and reduce downstream regret. Experiments on random linear programs and shortest-path problems show that our approach reduces regret, and accompanying theory characterizes properties of RCIFs and identifies regimes favorable to our method relative to baselines.

Title: Reducing SNAP Payment Errors at Lower Cost With AI: A Simulation Study
Authors: Alex Chohlas-Wood
Affiliations: New York University
Abstract: New federal legislation will require states with high payment error rates in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) to pay a share of benefit costs, potentially costing some states over a billion dollars per year. These costs create substantial pressure to improve payment accuracy. One strategy to improve payment accuracy is preauthorization review, in which staff double-check applications and correct mistakes before benefits are issued. But limited staff capacity makes it important to target these reviews effectively. One leading targeting approach uses statistical risk models to prioritize cases likely to contain errors. Another novel approach uses AI to flag specific potential discrepancies for reviewers to check. For states under pressure to reduce error rates, it is unclear which approach-or combination of approaches-would reduce payment error rates most effectively. We compare these strategies through simulations using public SNAP quality control data. Under our main assumptions, risk-based review alone costs about seven times as much as combining AI flags with risk scores. This cost advantage persists across a wide range of plausible assumptions. Our findings suggest that AI-assisted preauthorization review could be a key tool to help states avoid substantial cost-sharing obligations.

Title: Regret-Optimal Wasserstein-Robust Linear Regression
Authors: Sloan Nietert, Daniel Kühn
Affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne
Abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case risk under distributional uncertainty, but its decisions can be suboptimal in terms of their excess risk, or regret. We study this gap for multivariate least-squares regression, assuming that the observed source law and unknown target law differ by an adversarial 2-Wasserstein perturbation of size $\varepsilon$. We first identify the asymptotic complexity of robust decision-making in the $\varepsilon \to 0$ limit, characterized by a problem-specific condition number $κ$. Here, a wide spectrum of simple algorithms, including DRO, achieve the instance-optimal rate of $O(κ\varepsilon^2)$. For fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, we prove that DRO still achieves the minimax rate if the problem has bounded residual effective rank. On the other hand, we identify significant failure modes where DRO is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors. Fortunately, we prove that two alternative procedures, minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR), attain the minimax rate. We derive an exact convex reformulation of MRO and an accelerated proximal algorithm for SNR, along with high-probability finite-sample guarantees. We support these theoretical results with numerical experiments separating the performance of MRO and SNR from DRO.

Title: Revisiting Learning to Delegate: LLM Discovered Heuristics for Large-Scale Vehicle Routing
Authors: Zhengyang Wang, Renfei Tan, Shuze Liu, David Simchi‐Levi
Abstract: Efficient vehicle routing is critical to logistics and transportation, yet solving large-scale capacitated vehicle routing problems (CVRP) remains computationally challenging due to their combinatorial complexity. One approach to solve large-scale vehicle routing optimization is to identify promising subproblems and then optimize them using solvers. In this paper, we propose a framework of automatic heuristic design (AHD) in which a large language model (LLM) autonomously refines heuristics for selecting subproblems, enabling effective optimization of large-scale CVRP instances. Compared to prior approaches that train task-specific neural networks to select among heuristically constructed subproblems, our method discovers generalizable, interpretable LLM-generated heuristics to directly construct subproblems. Experiments show that our approach achieves comparable in-distribution performance while outperforming neural network-based policies on out-of-distribution instances with large-scale problems.

Title: Risk-Based Auto-Deleveraging
Authors: Steven Campbell, Natascha Hey, Ciamac C. Moallemi, Marcel Nutz
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: Auto-deleveraging (ADL) mechanisms are a critical yet understudied component of risk management on cryptocurrency futures exchanges. When available margin and other loss-absorbing resources are insufficient to cover losses following large price moves, exchanges reduce positions and socialize losses among solvent participants via rule-based ADL protocols. We formulate ADL as an optimization problem that minimizes the exchange's risk of loss arising from future equity shortfalls. In a single-asset, isolated-margin setting, the \emph{minimax leverage} policy -- minimizing the maximum leverage among participants -- is optimal for all monotone risk measures. This policy has a transparent structure: positions are reduced first for the most highly levered accounts, and leverage is progressively equalized via a water-filling (or ``leverage-draining'') rule. The policy is distribution-free, wash-trade resistant, Sybil resistant, and path-independent. It provides a canonical and implementable benchmark for ADL design and clarifies the economic logic underlying queue-based mechanisms used in practice. We further study the multi-asset, cross-margin setting, where the ADL problem becomes genuinely multi-dimensional: the exchange must allocate reductions across accounts with portfolios exposed to correlated price moves. Under the expected loss objective, asset-level shadow prices separate the problem across accounts, yielding a scalable numerical method. Naive gross leverage misleads here, ignoring within-portfolio hedging. When prices are driven by a single risk factor, the optimal policy is again water-filling, but in a factor-adjusted leverage, so better-hedged portfolios are deleveraged less. We apply the framework to the October~10, 2025 Hyperliquid ADL event. Relative to the exchange's realized allocation, our risk-minimizing allocations achieve lower expected shortfall.

Title: Robust Markov Decision Processes on Continuous State Spaces
Authors: Mengmeng Li, Yifan Hu, Daniel Kühn, Yan LI
Affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne; Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey; Texas A&M University
Abstract: We study infinite-horizon robust Markov decision processes (MDPs) on continuous state spaces with structured rectangular ambiguity set. The proposed ambiguity set falls within the convex hull of unknown generating kernels. We utilize the dynamic formulation of the corresponding robust MDPs, and subsequently introduce a stochastic first-order method for robust policy evaluation. We establish its high probability convergence to the robust value function, which in turn leads to an $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(1/ε^2)$ sample complexity. This high probability accuracy certificate is then used in an approximate policy iteration method that finds an $ε$-optimal policy with $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(1/ε^2)$ samples. The obtained sample complexities for both robust policy evaluation and optimization appear to be new for robust MDPs with continuous state spaces. Of independent interest, the proposed method is also directly applicable to zero-sum Markov games, which seems to strictly improve the existing sample complexities for continuous state spaces.

Title: Robustifying and Selecting Cohort-Appropriate Prognostic Models under Distributional Shifts
Authors: Dimitris Bertsimas, Carol Gao, Angelos Georgios Koulouras, Georgios Antonios Margonis
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
Abstract: External validation is widely regarded as the gold standard for prognostic model evaluation. In this study, we challenge the assumption that successful external calibration guarantees model generalizability and propose two complementary strategies to improve transportability of prognostic models across cohorts. Using six real-world surgical cohorts from tertiary academic centers, we tested whether successful external calibration depends largely on similarity in covariates and outcomes between training and validation cohorts, quantified using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, with calibration assessed by the Integrated Calibration Index (ICI). From the model-developer's perspective, we trained the "best-on-average" prognostic model by tuning toward a meta-analysis-derived covariate and outcome distribution as an approximation of the broader target population. From the end-user perspective, we proposed a simple measure for cohort outcome similarity to identify, among published models, the one most suitable for a given target cohort in terms of both calibration and clinical utility. External calibration worsened as distributional mismatch increased. Higher KL divergence was associated with higher ICI in both surgery-alone (Spearman $ρ=0.614$, $p=0.004$) and surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy cohorts (Spearman $ρ=0.738$, $p<0.001$). Meta-analysis-informed weighting improved calibration in most settings without materially affecting discrimination, with the clearest benefit when evaluated on the aggregated external population ($p=0.037$). Models developed in more similar cohorts achieved lower ICI in surgery-alone (Spearman $ρ=0.803$, $p<0.001$) and surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy cohorts (Spearman $ρ=0.737$, $p<0.001$), and provided greater clinical utility on DCA.

Title: Rule-Based Pricing Algorithms and Market Outcomes: An Experimental Study
Authors: Adrian Hillenbrand, Hans‐Theo Normann, Matthias Potarca, Tobias Werner
Affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology; Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf; National University of Ireland, Maynooth
Abstract: Rule-based pricing tools are widespread in digital commerce, yet we know little about how their design shapes market outcomes. In a controlled market experiment, participants use dashboards to build pricing algorithms competing in a sequential Bertrand game over multiple periods. We vary design features commonly found in commercial repricing tools: warnings about price wars, pre-configured strategies, and advice from a large language model. Most treatment variations raise market prices with effects driven by an increase in starting prices and more cooperative algorithm designs. The results matter for competition policy, platform regulation and current discussions on regulating algorithm design tools.

Title: SOTA or Luck? The Winner's Curse in LLM Leaderboards
Authors: Sikun Xu, Raphael Thomadsen, Dennis Zhang, Heng Zhang
Affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis; Arizona State University
Abstract: Public LLM leaderboards guide model evaluation and adoption, yet the reported performance of top-ranked models can be systematically overstated. This leaderboard winner's curse arises because ranking noisy benchmark scores rewards sampling luck alongside genuine ability. The same selection effect can distort scores throughout the leaderboard, a phenomenon we call the rank-induced bias. We develop an $m$-out-of-$N$ bootstrap to correct for this bias. It assumes a fixed model pool with independent, identically distributed bounded tasks while allowing arbitrary within-task correlation among models. Under exact population tiers separated by positive gaps, we prove that the bootstrap reduces $Θ(N^{-1/2})$ ranking bias to expected residual bias $o(N^{-1/2})$. Across 14 benchmarks from 5 benchmark families, the rank-1 adjustments range from approximately 0.09 to 3.86 percentage points. In our SWE-bench Verified snapshot, the tied leaders receive an adjustment of 0.90 percentage points. Such overstatement is large enough to make the apparent winner statistically fragile. Thus, we use the same bootstrap to further quantify the intervals of plausible rank positions for each model and group models into tiers. We establish sufficient conditions for consistent recovery of population tiers. On SWE-bench Verified, this procedure places 13 of 173 models in the leading tier. We combine the score adjustment and rank intervals in the Rank Uncertainty and Leaderboard Evaluation Report (RULER). We validate its finite-sample performance using sample splitting and calibrated simulations, and advocate publishing RULER alongside raw rankings so readers can assess both reported performance and the precision of the ordering. RULER also provides guidance for benchmark design that accounts for selection effects and ranking uncertainty.

Title: Safe Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning: Zero Constraint Violation and Primal-Averaging Convergence
Authors: Chenxi Li, Yao Shu, Siyang Gao, Shuang Qiu, Guangxin Jiang
Affiliations: Harbin Institute of Technology; City University of Hong Kong
Abstract: Many applications of multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) require policies that balance conflicting objectives while satisfying safety constraints. We study safe MORL with zero constraint violation throughout learning, covering both cumulative and stepwise constraints. A key challenge is to explore sufficiently under unknown dynamics and constraint costs without violating the constraints. For a given preference over objectives, we develop an algorithm to learn a safe Pareto optimal policy by combining optimistic reward estimates with pessimistic cost bounds. With high probability, every policy executed over $T$ episodes incurs zero constraint violation. The algorithm returns a safe Markov policy induced by the averaged occupancy measure and achieves an $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ suboptimality gap under smooth Tchebycheff scalarization. We further develop a preference-free algorithm that first explores safely without a prespecified preference and then computes a safe policy for any given preference without further interaction. Over $T$ exploration episodes and $K$ planning iterations, it retains the same safety guarantee and achieves an $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{T}+1/\sqrt{K})$ suboptimality gap. Both algorithms require knowledge of a policy that strictly satisfies the constraints and its costs. We then relax these requirements, incurring at most constant cumulative violation. To our knowledge, we provide the first sample-efficient MORL algorithms that guarantee safety for every executed policy.

Title: Sample Complexity of Peer Prediction
Authors: Abdellah Aznag, Robin Bowers, Rachel Cummings, Jason D. Hartline, Matthew vonAllmen, Bo Waggoner
Affiliations: Columbia University; University of Colorado Boulder; Northwestern University
Abstract: Peer prediction seeks to incentivize agents to truthfully report an observed signal by rewarding joint sets of reports without observing a ground truth. Following the generalization of information-theoretic mutual information introduced in Kong and Schoenebeck (2019), we call a function of a joint distribution over signals a mutual information when it is non-negative and disincentivizes garbling reports for all information structures. An unbiased estimator for a mutual information takes some number of samples from the distribution and returns rewards for both agents, such that the expected reward is equal to the mutual information. We seek to characterize the set of mutual informations with unbiased estimators for a given number of samples. We show that for three or fewer sampled report pairs, the only mutual information with an unbiased estimator is trivially zero, and for four or five samples with a binary report space, the Determinant Mutual Information (DMI) of Kong (2024) is the unique mutual information (up to a scalar multiple). We further show that DMI ceases to be unique at six samples. We provide an improved estimator of DMI for any given number of samples and characterize its convergence rate. We also examine mutual information estimators that accept a randomized number of samples. First, we show that mutual information estimators on an ex-ante bounded number of samples (termed "stop-short estimators") can achieve a lower variance than an equivalent fixed-sample estimator (for DMI). Second, we introduce the class of scoring-rule-based mutual informations and identify in this family a mutual information that can be estimated with under three samples in expectation.

Title: Scalable Evaluation of Medical AI using Evidence-based Practice Recommendations
Authors: Teya S. Bergamaschi, Bijal Rajput, Akshay Goel, Matthew Thompson, Jacqueline Baras Shreibati, Dave Steiner, Ashley Carrick, Mahvish Nagda, Dale R. Webster, Avinatan Hassidim, Katherine Chou, Yossi Matias, Po-Hsuan Cameron Chen, Christina Chen, Mike Schaekermann, Yun Liu, Anil K. Palepu
Abstract: Rigorously evaluating medical artificial intelligence (AI) requires testing open-ended clinical management across diverse presentations and stages of care. However, existing benchmarks rely on manual expert authoring, limiting coverage across conditions, conditional care pathways, and evolving guidelines. We develop an automated pipeline that extracts and verifies structured clinical criteria and branching decision trees from practice recommendations to generate scenarios spanning the care continuum, including nuanced presentations and practice variations across regions and guideline editions. Applied to 436 BMJ Best Practice clinical monographs (354 US, 82 International), this yields 3,200 scenarios spanning differential diagnosis, investigations, treatment, and complications, plus targeted suites for regional specificity (731 US/International pairs) and temporal freshness (630 scenarios). To grade responses, we develop a clinician-calibrated autorater that scores management plans on a 4-point rubric stratifying deviations by clinical severity. Across Gemini models, scaling improves adherence, while web search (+0.8 percentage points [pp] on average) and multi-sample synthesis (+2.2 pp) combine additively (+2.8 pp). In context, full monographs consistently trail condensed excerpts. On targeted suites, web search narrows international performance gaps (+4.2 pp) and improves adherence to newly updated guidance (+4.6 pp). In a study with Primary Care Physicians (n = 9) across 200 scenarios, AI assistance raises adherence from 50.5% to 70.0%, driven largely by fewer clinical omissions. Overall, our results demonstrate a scalable evaluation setup using an evidence-based corpus originally written to guide human clinical decision-making, and demonstrate its viability to assess medical AI and its assistance on clinician decision-making.

Title: Scheduling in Cloud,Fog, and Edge Computing: A Comparative Analysis and Decision Framework for Technique Selection
Authors: Rana Ghazali, Douglas G. Down
Affiliations: McMaster University
Abstract: The increasing heterogeneity and dynamism of cloud, fog, and edge computing make scheduling a challenging problem involving diverse resource capabilities, workload characteristics, latency and energy constraints, and competing optimization objectives. Although numerous scheduling methods have been proposed, existing reviews often provide fragmented coverage of computing environments, scheduling granularities, or technique families, offering limited guidance on selecting an appropriate approach for specific requirements. This review presents a comparative analysis of task, job, and workflow scheduling across the cloud, fog, and edge paradigms, covering heuristic, metaheuristic, learning-based, and hybrid techniques. Studies published between 2020 and 2026 are analyzed according to scheduling granularity, computing environment, optimization objectives, constraints, performance metrics, and evaluation tools. The analysis highlights trade-offs among computational efficiency, optimization capability, adaptability, and implementation complexity across technique families. Heuristic methods offer low computational overhead for relatively stable scheduling conditions, whereas metaheuristic methods are suited to complex and multi-objective optimization problems. Learning-based methods provide greater adaptability to dynamic and uncertain environments but introduce data, training, inference, and convergence requirements. Hybrid methods combine complementary capabilities but generally increase computational and implementation complexity. Based on these findings, a decision framework is developed to guide technique selection according to workload characteristics, environmental conditions, optimization objectives, resource constraints, and computational requirements.

Title: Semantic Representation for Agentic Self-Play in Automated Laboratories
Authors: Yves Delley, John Coller, Zachary Cutts, Alexander Daryin, Mathias M. J. Bellaiche, Jun Woo Kim, Oscar Donosa, Srinidhi B. Seshadri, Tanner Clary, Sandy Klemm, Avinatan Hassidim, Yossi Matias, Pooja Rao, Petar Sirkovic, Annalisa Pawlosky
Affiliations: Google (United States)
Abstract: Navigating complex, high-dimensional biological search spaces necessitates scalable physical and computational intelligence to explore beyond local optima through iterative self-play across ideation, experimentation, and automation. Translating experimental designs into reliable physical execution remains bottlenecked by static laboratory automation and unmodeled physical variability. To address this, we introduce VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories, or VERID, a foundational infrastructure designed to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of artificial intelligence (AI) agents and complex, error-prone physical realities of wet labs. VERID is a persistent, high-fidelity semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell that provides four core services: queryable introspection for agentic reasoning, time-compressed simulation for protocol validation, comprehensive trace persistence for a complete scientific record, and a framework for safe execution. We present three case studies using aqueous dye and deionized water mixtures to validate the optical and fluidic foundations of VERID. These studies demonstrate how VERID enables pre-emptive detection of critical errors in experimental protocols, stateful mid-run error recovery and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures. The simulation functions as a discrete accounting engine, allowing agents to safely and inexpensively explore experimental designs in silico and refine experimental strategies through iterative self-play. VERID also captures structured multimodal experimental data for downstream analysis, knowledge mining and agent training. We argue that this semantic layer is an essential prerequisite for deploying autonomous agents in the biochemical and biomedical sciences, ensuring data integrity, operational safety, and paving the way for tackling previously intractable grand challenges in biology.

Title: Semiparametric Efficiency in Sequential Experiments: Characterization and Design via Average Propensity
Authors: Jiachun Li, David Simchi‐Levi
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Modern experiments, including evaluations of AI-enabled services and platform interventions, often depart from independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sampling because assignments may be adaptive, balanced across covariates, or subject to rollout constraints such as exposure, fairness, and budget limits. This paper studies the efficiency benchmark for estimating causal targets in such sequential experiments. We show that every non-anticipating design induces an average propensity score, and we establish a semiparametric lower bound: for regular locally unbiased estimators, attainable precision is bounded by the i.i.d. efficiency benchmark evaluated at this induced score. The average propensity score thereby serves as a common benchmark and design target, allowing sequential experimental design to be viewed as choosing or learning an efficient allocation rule, with operational constraints entering through the admissible set when present. We then develop implementable batched adaptive designs that approach this benchmark through two complementary mechanisms. The first uses regression adjustment based on efficient influence functions; for general smooth estimands it attains the benchmark under standard nuisance-rate conditions, while for linear functionals of outcome means it achieves a sharp second-order rate. The second uses adaptive covariate balancing to attain the same benchmark through the assignment mechanism, enabling simple moment-based estimation. Both routes require only a small number of policy updates, making them compatible with delayed feedback and easier to monitor in operational deployments. Numerical experiments and an empirical study of AI medical-assistant evaluation demonstrate the practical efficiency gains, including in multi-treatment settings. Overall, the paper provides a unified framework for characterizing and designing efficient sequential experiments.

Title: Separate versus Pooled Winsorization in Difference-in-Differences: Bias, Efficiency, and Finite-Sample Guarantees
Authors: Yukai Huang, Chao Cheng, Chenshan Hu
Affiliations: Suffolk University; University of Washington; University of Colorado Boulder

Title: Setting Optimal Reserve Prices using Fine-Tuned Language Models
Authors: Joshua R. Foster, Fredrik Ødegaard
Affiliations: Western University

Title: Settling the Approximability of Submodular Facility Location
Authors: Adam N. Elmachtoub, Bento Natura, Meike Neuwohner
Affiliations: Columbia University; Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique
Abstract: In submodular facility location (SFL), introduced by Svitkina and Tardos (SODA 2006), clients $\mathcal{C}$ in a metric space are assigned to facilities $\mathcal{F}$. A facility serving a set $S \subseteq \cal C$ of clients incurs cost $g(S)$, where $g$ is a monotone submodular function common to all facilities. The best known approximation factor for SFL is $O(\log\log|\mathcal{C}|)$, due to Abbasi, Adamczyk, Bosch-Calvo, Byrka, Grandoni, Sornat, and Tinguely (ICALP 2024), improving on the $O(\log|\mathcal{C}|)$-approximation of Svitkina and Tardos. We show that this is best possible up to a constant factor in the value-oracle model by showing that there exists no algorithm with only polynomially many queries to $g$ with approximation ratio $o(\log\log|\mathcal{C}|)$. This bound holds for algorithms with unlimited computation time, and when $g$ is restricted to matroid rank functions. We also show that the natural linear programming relaxation has an integrality gap of $Θ(\log\log|\mathcal{C}|)$. Our lower bound follows by constructing an extension of Vondrák's symmetry-gap approach (FOCS 2009) for matroid rank functions.

Title: Sharp Covering-Number Bounds for Feedforward ReLU Networks via Parameter Symmetries
Authors: Ruizhi Deng, Guohao Shen, Tangrui Xiong
Affiliations: Hong Kong Polytechnic University
Abstract: In neural networks, distinct parameter configurations often realize the same input--output mapping, indicating that nominal parameter counts can overstate functional complexity. In this paper, we characterize the parameter-space symmetries of ReLU and Leaky ReLU networks across fully connected, convolutional, and residual architectures. We prove that every quasianalytic parameter map preserving the network function is a composition of positive channel scaling and channel permutation. By quotienting out both symmetries, we derive uniform covering-number upper bounds in which positive scaling reduces the complexity exponent from the total parameter count $S$ to $S-H$ (with $H$ denoting the number of scalable channels) and permutation symmetry divides the bound by the factorial count $G$ of channel permutations. We establish matching lower bounds showing that the exponent $S-H$ is sharp in general and that the divisor $G$ is attained for one-hidden-layer and generically identifiable networks. We further extend these results to general continuous piecewise-linear activated networks. Finally, we apply our covering-number bounds to derive statistical risk guarantees for empirical risk minimization and capacity control beyond i.i.d.\ settings, and show how the underlying symmetries help explain weight rebalancing in function approximation and flat directions in empirical risk optimization.

Title: SmartEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-Generated Smart Contracts from Natural Language Specifications
Authors: Abhinav Goel, Agostino Capponi, Alfio Gliozzo, Chaitya Shah
Affiliations: Columbia University; IBM (United States)
Abstract: We introduce SmartEval, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the quality of Solidity smart contracts generated by large language models (LLMs) from natural language specifications. SmartEval provides a corpus of 9,000 generated contracts paired with expert-written ground-truth implementations drawn from the FSMSCG dataset, a five-dimensional evaluation rubric covering functional completeness, variable fidelity, state-machine correctness, business-logic fidelity, and code quality, and a reproducible generation-and-evaluation pipeline. To validate the benchmark's reliability, we conduct three independent empirical studies: a five-condition ablation study (N=300 per condition) isolating the contribution of each pipeline component, a human expert evaluation by three Columbia University PhD researchers confirming automated scores align with expert judgment to within 0.34 points, and external security analysis via the Slither static analyzer confirming 79.4% agreement between the LLM auditor and a non-LLM rule-based tool. Systematic analysis of 9,000 generated contracts reveals characteristic failure modes (logic omissions at 35.3%, state transition errors at 23.4%, and complexity-driven degradation) and quantifies a +8.29 composite-score advantage of generated contracts over ground-truth implementations, attributable to LLMs' literal specification-following behavior. SmartEval establishes a reproducible, validated foundation for empirical research on LLM smart contract synthesis quality, with all data, evaluation code, and generated contracts publicly released.

Title: Spec2Twin-Chain: Orchestrating Bi-Level Optimization with LLMs for Blockchain Digital Twin Construction
Authors: Haoting Zhang, Haoxian Chen, Jiayuan Sheng, Donglin Zhan, Zeyu Zheng, David D. W. Yao, Wenpin Tang
Abstract: Building a blockchain digital twin largely requires translating domain knowledge and specific system descriptions into a simulator architecture, calibrating its parameters against behavioral evidence, and validating the constructed twin. These steps are commonly performed through application-specific modeling efforts that can be difficult to reuse across systems and downstream decision problems. We consider automating this process through Spec2Twin-Chain, a framework that formulates blockchain digital-twin construction as a bi-level optimization problem. At the upper level, a large language model proposes and revises structurally admissible architectures using system specifications, behavioral evidence, and feedback from evaluated designs. At the lower level, a simulation-based optimizer calibrates the architecture-conditioned parameters under explicit objectives and guardrail constraints. The two levels iterate. The evaluated candidates at lower levels are retained in a global archive and used to guide subsequent proposals at upper levels. We conduct controlled experiments involving twin calibration, feedback-driven recovery, stress analysis, downstream policy optimization, and policy updating. The results demonstrate that the framework can construct behaviorally accurate twins, improve initial designs through iterative feedback, and reuse calibrated twins to support downstream decisions.

Title: Specifying Reward Functions for RL Without Environment Sampling
Authors: Stephane Hatgis-Kessell, W. Bradley Knox, Emma Brunskill
Affiliations: Stanford University; The University of Texas at Austin
Abstract: Enabling human stakeholders to specify reward functions that lead to their desired outcomes is a key challenge in deploying reinforcement learning agents. Preference-based methods such as online RLHF can reduce the burden of manual reward design, but they require repeatedly training policies, sampling trajectories from the real world, and eliciting feedback, making them impractical in settings where environment interaction is computationally expensive or unsafe. We introduce Experience-Free Autonomous Reward Specification (EARS), a method for learning reward functions from preferences without environment interaction. Our approach uses a structured LLM-mediated process to construct a small set of expressive reward features from a task description and the environment observation space, then strategically samples imagined trajectories in this feature space and learns feature weights from preferences over the imagined trajectory pairs. We evaluate on three long-horizon domains: pandemic lockdown regulation design, insulin administration for diabetes patients, and autonomous vehicle control on a highway. We compare EARS to baselines that also enable reward specification without environment interaction--namely, methods that directly prompt an LLM to generate a reward function. When learning from either ground-truth preference labels or preferences labeled by a LLM, EARS designs reward functions that are more aligned with the ground truth reward function that produced the preferences or LLM context than these baselines. These results suggest that preference-based reward specification remains effective without environment sampling, enabling practical reward design in settings where collecting real trajectories is costly or infeasible.

Title: Spectral Scaling Laws of Muon
Authors: Gagik Magakyan, Pablo A. Parrilo, Asuman Ozdaglar
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Orthonormalized update rules have rapidly become a leading choice of optimizer for training large language models, with recent open-source state-of-the-art models adopting Muon. To keep these updates tractable, Muon performs the orthonormalization with the Newton--Schulz (NS) iteration. Since NS is only approximate, directions with small singular values fail to be orthonormalized. In Muon, NS is applied to the momentum matrix at every step, yet little is known about how the singular value spectrum of these momentum matrices behaves during training, or how that behavior changes with model size. We present the first systematic study of this question. Tracking singular value quantiles of the momentum buffer across layers in models ranging from 77M to 2.8B parameters, we observe a consistent picture: after a short burn-in, the quantiles stabilize at a value determined by the layer type and model size. These stabilization values follow remarkably clean power laws in model size, with layer-dependent exponents. Layers up to mid-late depth scale very mildly with model size $M$ (around $M^{-0.25}$), so the standard 5-step NS configuration used at academic scale will continue to orthonormalize them at much larger scales. Some of the late layers, however, scale much more aggressively (up to $M^{-0.96}$) and will fall into the NS failure regime at frontier scale unless one uses more NS iterations or better-tuned coefficients. NS iterations are computationally expensive at scale; our laws give practitioners a principled, layer-aware recipe for choosing the minimum NS configuration that still orthonormalizes the directions that matter -- avoiding unnecessary computation without sacrificing update quality.

Title: Stablecoin Integration and Stress Transmission Through Crypto-Asset Service Providers: Evidence from Austria
Authors: Pietro Saggese, Michael Sigmund, Burkhard Raunig, Esther Segalla, Bernhard Haslhofer, Christos Andreas Makridis
Affiliations: IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca; National Bank of Austria; Complexity Science Hub
Abstract: Stablecoins are increasingly entangled with traditional finance, making their response to stress a financial stability concern. However, blockchain pseudonymity and the lack of geographic identifiers force existing work to rely on indirect proxies to infer and locate market participants. In this paper, we exploit a regulatory registry that directly identifies the on-chain addresses of every crypto-asset service provider (CASP) registered in Austria at the end of 2024, reconstructing their Bitcoin, Ether, USDT, and USDC activity through May 2025. Austrian CASPs intermediate roughly $30 billion in cumulative external transfers, while transfers among them are negligible. Combining two transaction-level signals, interaction with CASP cold wallets and on-chain transaction frequency, we classify CASP counterparty activity as retail-like or institutionally mediated. Around stress events, the two groups exhibit distinct flow responses that are obscured in aggregate data. After the FTX bankruptcy, we observe retail-like withdrawals and institutional deposits across assets. After Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) failure, retail-like USDC deposits and institutionally mediated withdrawals are consistent with USDC's asymmetric redemption access. Registry-based, transaction-level measurements thus offer a reproducible basis for cross-jurisdictional monitoring of how cryptoasset markets transmit risk.

Title: Statistical robustness and time consistency in risk averse optimization
Authors: Alexander Shapiro, Yan Li
Affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology; Texas A&M University
Abstract: The aim of this manuscript is to investigate risk measures which are not necessarily convex. We show that law invariant coherent risk measures are not robust with respect to contamination of the probability measure, in the sense that an arbitrarily small contamination can change their values by an arbitrary amount. This contrasts with the Value-at-Risk, which is robust against such contamination. In addition, we show that for a given law invariant risk measure and a given policy, one can construct, under mild conditions, conditional risk measures with respect to which this policy is time consistent, in the frameworks of both Markov Decision Processes and Stochastic Optimal Control.

Title: Strategic Origins of Network Structure
Authors: Christoph Riedl, Rory Smead
Affiliations: Northeastern University
Abstract: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.

Title: Subsidizing Sequential Search
Authors: Salvador Candelas, Nicole Immorlica, Brendan Lucier
Affiliations: Pennsylvania State University; Microsoft (United States); Microsoft Research (United Kingdom)
Abstract: We study markets where firms compete for consumer attention by subsidizing costly product inspection. These subsidies do not change product quality, but they alter the order in which consumers search by lowering inspection costs. We establish a subsidy-sorting principle: in any equilibrium, higher-quality firms provide weakly larger subsidies, leading consumers to search in descending subsidy order. A unique equilibrium survives forward-induction reasoning in the spirit of the Intuitive Criterion: low-quality firms are never inspected, intermediate-quality firms separate with strictly increasing subsidies, and high-quality firms pool at the full subsidy. This equilibrium maximizes information revelation among all possible outcomes and ensures efficient inspection. We then extend the analysis to AI-mediated platforms that can create and price inspection tokens. The platform's optimal linear pricing leads to excessive inspection relative to the social optimum. While this distortion does not reduce consumer welfare, it reallocates surplus from sellers to the platform and consumers.

Title: Synthetic Nearest Neighbors: Extending Synthetic Controls for Matrix Completion with Missing Not at Random Data
Authors: Anish Agarwal, Munther A. Dahleh, Devavrat Shah, Dennis Shen
Affiliations: Columbia University; Massachusetts Institute of Technology; University of Southern California
Abstract: We develop a causal framework for matrix completion under missing not at random (MNAR) data. Drawing on synthetic controls from the econometric panel data literature, our approach relaxes two assumptions common in MNAR matrix completion: positivity and independence of observation indicators. Unlike traditional panel data models, which often require prescribed block-sparse geometries, our framework accommodates flexible, heterogeneous observation patterns through target-specific local information structures. We propose synthetic nearest neighbors (SNN), a local synthetic-controls-inspired estimator, and establish finite-sample entrywise error bounds and consistency for mean recovery under suitable conditions. We further derive asymptotic normality under heteroskedastic noise and develop feasible entrywise inference. To estimate entry-specific noise variances, we apply the same local principle to squared outcomes, obtaining consistency under bounded noise and asymptotic unbiasedness under general subgaussian noise. Simulation studies corroborate the theoretical findings across a range of missingness designs and observation patterns.

Title: TRACE: Governing AI-Assisted Research with Principles from Computer Science
Authors: Amirhossein Zohrehvand, Aldona Kapacinskaite
Affiliations: INSEAD
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has made it easier than ever to produce research outputs. Adding an agentic tool to a research team's work potentially extends the team's capabilities but calls for an active approach to organizing the research process. The pressing question, therefore, is how research teams should organize their work with this technology. We contend that the question is not new: software engineering and security research have long studied how teams of people working with machines keep control of projects with many contributors. We distill principles from the practices these literatures report and transpose them to AI-assisted research. The principles form TRACE: Track records, Review against sources, Accept independently, Control transitions, and Evaluate corrections. Together, the five principles give researchers a common basis for remaining in control while integrating AI into their workflows. By bounding units of work and attending to how each is shaped, they can help researchers pace AI-assisted work to human attention rather than to the speed at which AI produces content. We also introduce TRACE-OS, an operating system for AI-assisted research projects. It puts the principles into practice through shared instructions, tools, and records that fit researchers' existing workflows. With TRACE, we aim to join a conversation about the governing principles through which the research community can benefit from AI. We contend that a simple enough and useful standard can contribute to harnessing AI capabilities, allowing teams to delegate parts of their work to AI, while also building trust within teams and the broader research community.

Title: Tabular Foundation Models for Credit Risk Prediction: A Dedicated Review and Empirical Comparison
Authors: Bart Baesens, Andreas Goethals, Stefan Lessmann, Simon De Vos, Cristián Bravo, David Martens, Victor Medina-Olivares, Christophe Mues, María Óskarsdóttir, Seppe vanden Broucke, Tony Van Gestel, Tim Verdonck, Wouter Verbeke
Affiliations: KU Leuven; Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin; Western University; University of Antwerp; University of Edinburgh; University of Southampton; Ghent University
Abstract: Predictive models are central to credit risk management, where the accuracy of default-probability and loss estimates affects the profitability of lending and the stability of the financial system. Decades of benchmarking research have consolidated the state of the art, with gradient-boosting models often representing the strongest machine-learning benchmark, while linear and logistic models remain important regulatory and industry reference models. The recent advent of tabular data foundation models introduces a new paradigm for predictive modeling. Rather than fitting a model to a target dataset, they use in-context learning to integrate information from the target dataset with prior knowledge acquired through large-scale pretraining on diverse collections of (synthetic) tabular data. We conjecture that access to information beyond the target data is beneficial in small-data settings and may help address longstanding challenges, including low-default portfolios. Whether this promise holds in practice remains an open question. This paper benchmarks state-of-the-art tabular foundation models against a broad set of classical and advanced machine learning competitors on two core tasks: Probability of Default (PD) and Loss Given Default (LGD) modeling. We evaluate $33$ classification methods across $14$ PD datasets and $27$ regression methods across $7$ LGD datasets, spanning a range of performance indicators and experimental conditions. The most recent tabular foundation models, in particular TabPFN-3 and TabICLv2, achieve the strongest average results, with the largest gains in small-sample and strongly imbalanced settings. These results are notable because these models are used with their pretrained parameters fixed and without downstream hyperparameter optimization or task-specific parameter updates.

Title: Tabular Foundation Models in Financial Predictions
Authors: Ed deHaan, Allen Huang
Affiliations: Stanford University; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

Title: TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information
Authors: Chanwoo Park, J. H. Jeong, Zachary Wojtowicz, Yubin Kim, Taekyun Lee, Kaiqing Zhang, Asuman Ozdaglar
Abstract: Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants. Yet AI agents are still primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation. We introduce TeamGym, an environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making problems constructed from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. TeamGym introduces a method to identify a minimal set of facts, each element of which is necessary and all of which are collectively sufficient for a correct final decision, which we call pivotal information. This enables TeamGym to both control the distribution of pivotal information and track how well agents identify and integrate pivotal information when making team decisions. Examining 8 language models on 12 source corpora, we find that current AI agents often fail to effectively share information: Distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average relative to giving the same information to a single model (a communication gap). We also document that participants do not effectively retrieve decision-relevant information on their own: A team's success rate is lowered by a further 19.9 points when participants must identify and extract pivotal information from source material rather than receiving it directly (a retrieval gap). To help remedy these deficits, we use TeamGym to train policies through reinforcement learning on team decision loss. Across two policy-training experiments, we find that training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.

Title: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
Authors: Andrew W. Lo, Chaoyi Zhao
Affiliations: Santa Fe Institute; Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

Title: The Complexity of Computing a Competitive Equilibrium in Fisher Markets with Chores
Authors: Christian Kroer, Ruta Mehta, Tianlong Nan
Affiliations: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; Columbia University
Abstract: We study the complexity of computing competitive equilibria in Fisher markets with divisible chores and positive rational disutility coefficients and earning requirements. For linear disutilities, we prove that exact equilibrium computation is CLS-complete. In particular, the problem remains CLS-hard even when the earning requirements are binary in $1$ and $2^k$, where $k$ is an integer. We prove hardness by encoding the first-order conditions of a box-constrained quadratic program in equilibrium prices and earning flows, using a compact minimum-cost flow construction. For convex constant-elasticity-of-substitution (CES) disutilities, exact equilibrium prices may be irrational. We formulate the problem of finite-precision equilibrium price computation, in which we seek rational prices with a certified market clearing error at most a given rational tolerance encoded in binary. We prove that this problem is CLS-complete for every fixed rational exponent $ρ>1$. To prove this hardness, we encode a quartic polynomial through the fourth-order expansion of the CES price potential function corresponding to the Eisenberg-Gale (EG) dual program, and show that every sufficiently accurate approximate equilibrium of the constructed market lies near uniform prices. Additionally, we also identify a tractable special case of chores Fisher markets. In particular, we provide a strongly polynomial algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in linear markets whose disutility matrix has rank at most two and earning requirements are arbitrary positive rationals. For $n$ agents and $m$ chores, the algorithm uses $O(nm(n+m))$ rational arithmetic operations and comparisons, with polynomial intermediate encoding length.

Title: The Data Debt of Stockouts: Partial Identification and Minimax-Regret Inventory Control
Authors: Jinbiao Chen, Shuang Jin, Hanzhang Qin
Affiliations: National University of Singapore
Abstract: Problem definition: Inventory decisions select which demand enters sales logs. Unrecorded forecasts can leave demand frequencies unidentified even when stocking levels are recorded. We study which multistage ordering decisions these logs can justify and what finite samples can guarantee. Methodology/results: Nested stockout thresholds yield exact sets of compatible demand laws and finite representations for policy evaluation. We choose one deterministic inventory rule to minimize its largest expected cost gap from the informed optimum under the same law. This population value is data debt for the specified information and policy class. Under independent demand, carryover can create positive debt despite common optimal actions in every isolated period. Finite samples add learning error above debt. The required sample count grows linearly with the selection bound, with upper and lower orders matching up to logarithmic factors. This rate requires fixed demand and cost bounds, sufficient revelation, and a uniformly positive probability of clearing all feasible stock across the confidence sets. Controlled and semi-synthetic studies separate policy improvements from tighter guarantees. Managerial implications: More records can tighten guarantees while debt persists. Deeper revelation can establish common optimality without fully identifying demand. Using these guarantees requires validated logging, a credible selection range, and a regret tolerance in cost units. Information acquisition must distinguish tighter assurance from operating savings.

Title: The Effects of Generative AI on Collaboration and Social Networks Among Knowledge Workers
Authors: Giuseppe Soda, Alessandro Iorio, Leonardo Rizzo
Affiliations: Bocconi University
Abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence has raised concerns that knowledge work may become less dependent on human-to-human interaction. Yet because AI-generated outputs require interpretation, verification, and social legitimation, generative AI may instead increase collaboration among workers. We test these competing predictions using passively collected behavioral data from more than 12,000 knowledge workers observed over 13 months during the staged organizational rollout of an AI-powered assistant (Microsoft Copilot). Using two complementary quasi-experimental designs -- a staggered difference-in-differences model and a fixed-effects instrumental-variable approach -- we estimate the effects of generative AI on workers' collaboration behavior and social network structure. We estimate that generative AI increased collaboration time across communication channels and reshaped individual networks. Those using generative AI interacted with more colleagues and their networks became less clustered, indicating broadening in collaboration structures. At the same time, they also concentrated more of their collaboration on ties with stronger prior histories, deepening reliance on already trusted colleagues. Together, these findings suggest that, while generative AI changes how people work, it may not displace human-to-human interactions.

Title: The Geography of (Concurrent) Block Proposing
Authors: Ciamac C. Moallemi, Mallesh M. Pai, Dan Robinson, Christoph Schlegel
Affiliations: Columbia University; Rice University
Abstract: The resilience and censorship resistance of a blockchain depend on where the validators and proposers of that blockchain physically operate. We study the economic incentives behind this location choice, both with a single proposer and with multiple concurrent proposers. Formally, we study a game where proposers first choose locations and then compete in a first-price auction for an opportunity whose common value is driven by information from geographically dispersed sources. A single proposer minimizes variance-weighted delay, locating at a weighted median of the sources and co-locating with any dominant one. By contrast, with two proposers, information both observe equally early earns no rent, and each proposer's expected profit is proportional to the standard deviation of the information it receives before its rival. We show that the location game admits the jointly unobserved variance as an ordinal potential, so global solutions of a weighted two-median problem are equilibria. With two sources, one proposer locates at each, however weak one is. With more proposers and at least as many sources, equilibrium locations are distinct under regular bidding. Multiple concurrent proposers thus do more than limit any single proposer's control over inclusion: by rewarding exclusive rather than shared information, they create an economic force toward geographic decentralization.

Title: The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models
Authors: Douglas Guilbeault, Bhargav Srinivasa Desikan
Affiliations: Stanford University; University of Oxford
Abstract: Conceptual abstraction and gender are two equally central aspects of the human mind, yet they have traditionally been studied in isolation from one another, as though they were fundamentally separate. Here, we find gender and abstraction are systematically linked throughout the space of concepts spanning single (N = 40,000) and multi-word expressions (N = 67,000): across billions of words and millions of images on the internet --- and across numerous measurement techniques, including human and AI classifications --- more abstract concepts are more associated with men, a pattern we show replicates in languages around the world. This male abstraction bias not only holds across semantic domains, but it also maps onto grammatical structure: verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded, revealing a system-wide trace of stereotypes accentuating agentic qualities in men. Furthermore, we show this bias readily emerges in the free associations humans and AIs produce in controlled online tasks, indicating its psychological internalization and its algorithmic reproduction. These findings identify a latent structure in conceptual space that unifies a range of stereotypes: for example, framings of women as more embodied, emotional, and warm, versus men as more cognitive, rational, and competent; as well as erroneous views of men as better at mathematics, science, and engineering. More broadly, by analyzing an unprecedentedly large, multimodal sample of online data, we provide culture-wide evidence of gender as a core organizing principle shaping conceptual space far beyond the characterization of people and social roles.

Title: The Optimal Competitive Ratio for Subadditive Online Combinatorial Auctions is Less Than 1/2
Authors: Andrés Cristi, J. Zhang
Affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne
Abstract: We construct a four-buyer online combinatorial auction with independent subadditive valuations and a fixed, known arrival order in which every online rule earns strictly less than $1/2$ of the expected offline optimum. A common partition, revealed at the third arrival, gives the first three buyers one unit of welfare per item. If the rule uses three distinct partitions, either an item allocated early contributes zero or the fourth buyer's expected value for the remaining bundle is one less than its size. We compute the optimal online and offline welfare exactly and show that a $1/2$ guarantee always holds with at most three buyers.

Title: The Pareto Secretary Problem
Authors: Andrés Cristi, Yilin Kong, J. Zhang
Affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne; Chinese University of Hong Kong
Abstract: The Pareto secretary problem asks for online selection of a Pareto-maximal observation from an i.i.d. sample: no other observation is at least as good in every coordinate and strictly better in one. For every fixed dimension $d\ge2$ and independent continuous coordinates, the optimal failure probability is of order $1/[(\log n)^{d-1}\log\log n]$, both with full information and with coordinate ranks alone. A deterministic rank rule attains the optimal leading term uniformly over the marginals. For every fixed positive definite Gaussian covariance, the same failure order holds, with a leading constant depending on the correlation matrix, and a rank-based rule attains the optimal leading failure probability without knowing the Gaussian parameters. In both models, we determine the optimal fixed cutoff and its leading failure constant; its failure probability exceeds the unrestricted optimum by a factor $Θ_d((\log\log n)^2)$. Under arbitrary dependence, a fixed joint density with uniform marginals can instead have optimal full-information success tending to approximately $0.58$. The proof uses the scarcity of observations with very small domination probability to bound every stopping rule. A matching rule selects a currently maximal point when this probability is below a threshold that increases as time runs out. Coordinate ranks from an initial sample provide sufficiently accurate estimates to preserve the optimal leading failure probability. For singular Gaussian distributions with known correlations, we characterize the optimal failure asymptotics attainable using ranks. Singular dependence can make every observation acceptable or recover the difficulty of selecting a single best point.

Title: Tight Guarantees for Static Policies in Vehicle Sharing Networks
Authors: Adam N. Elmachtoub, Jiaqi Shi
Affiliations: Columbia University
Abstract: We study pricing in a vehicle sharing network with $N$ locations and $C$ vehicles, motivated by on-demand bike, scooter, and car sharing, as well as robotaxi and ride sharing services. Customers request directed trips between locations, with travel times following general distributions, and leave without service if no vehicle is available. Pricing affects both demand for trips and the distribution of vehicles across locations. Computing an optimal dynamic pricing policy is challenging because the system state depends on the number of vehicles available at each location and in transit (including how long they have been traveling), motivating the use of simple static policies that offer a fixed price for each trip. For any number of vehicles and locations, we establish a tight performance guarantee for static pricing relative to optimal dynamic pricing. The guarantee holds for any concave objective functions (including revenue rate) and general travel time distributions. Our tight guarantee is bounded below by $ \frac{C}{C + \min \{ C -1, \sqrt{ CN} \} }$ (over 50%), achieving the first universal, non-asymptotic constant factor guarantee. We also prove that the optimal static policy can be efficiently computed by solving a convex optimization problem. Finally, we extend our performance guarantee to the setting with supply redirection.

Title: Tight Sequential Confidence Intervals for Online Kernel Regression
Authors: Haichen Hu, David Simchi‐Levi
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: We characterize, in the worst case over kernels, the sharp minimax width of online confidence intervals for elements of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). This resolves the open problem posed by Vakili et al. (2021) in its original discrete-time form. A learner observes $y_i=f(x_i)+ε_i$ at adaptively chosen points, with $\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B$ and i.i.d. $R$-sub-Gaussian noise, and reports the interval $|f(x)-μ_n(x)|\leρ_n(δ)σ_n(x)$, where $μ_n$ and $σ_n$ are the posterior mean and standard deviation of a surrogate Gaussian process model with regularization parameter $λ$. Writing $ρ_n^*(δ)$ for the minimax confidence width for a fixed kernel, we show that, for the sum of a linear kernel and a periodic Sobolev kernel, all sufficiently large $n$, and all $δ\in(0,1/4]$, $ρ_n^*(δ)\asymp B+(R/λ)\sqrt{γ_n+\log(1/δ)}$, where $γ_n$ is the maximal information gain and grows polynomially in $n$. Building on Lattimore (2023), we construct an adaptive design on a fixed two-dimensional domain for which, under Gaussian noise, the normalized error at a prespecified point is $Ω(B+(R/λ)\sqrt{γ_n})$ with constant probability. This rules out the conjectured polylogarithmic width in the worst case over kernels and online designs.

Title: Too Late to Prune: Generative AI, the Screen, and Team Creative Decisions
Authors: Difang Huang, Shumin Yu, Fadong Chen, Weihua Zhou
Affiliations: Chinese Academy of Sciences; Zhejiang University

Title: Toward an AI-Powered Computational Testbed for Workforce Policy
Authors: Sumer Sumeet Vaid, Ashley V. Whillans
Affiliations: Harvard University
Abstract: Workforce transformations are difficult to forecast and costly to mismanage. In particular, the integration of artificial intelligence into knowledge work currently affects a substantial share of the global workforce, yet this transition proceeds without tools to forecast how individual employees will respond psychologically and behaviorally. We combine recent advances in LLM-powered generative agents with foundational management science and organizational behavior research to propose dynamic employee agents. Among consenting populations, these agents can be seeded with HR records, validated psychometric measures, and digital activity data to simulate employees' cognitive, emotional, and behavioral trajectories across successive workdays during planned organizational changes. In this article, we detail the computational architecture required to construct this simulation platform and define the privacy, accuracy, and representativeness safeguards necessary for responsible deployment. We argue that establishing this prospective forecasting infrastructure is a critical technical requirement for managing the current global workforce realignment around AI.

Title: Training and Evaluating Diffusion Policies with Long Context Lengths
Authors: Abhinav Agarwal, Adam Wei, Taylan Kargin, Michael Zeng, Cole Becker, Arif Kerem Dayı, Pablo A. Parrilo, Asuman Ozdaglar, Russ Tedrake
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Imitation learning has enabled highly-dexterous robotic manipulation from RGB observations. Policies trained with these methods, however, typically condition robot actions on only a short history of observations. These policies cannot solve tasks that require memory and can get stuck repeatedly executing the same failing motions. In this work, we first benchmark policy performance as context length is incrementally increased from short to long, across a spectrum of tasks with varying local stability and memory requirements, and in multiple data regimes. To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate context length for Diffusion Policies at this level of detail. Our results challenge prior claims: naively scaling context length is not as brittle as advertised in literature. With an appropriate conditioning method and denoising backbone (UNet+Cross-Attention), single-task policies achieve high success rates on many tasks in the usual data regime even with naive scaling. Next, we propose a training algorithm to jointly train policies at multiple context lengths, further reducing the sample complexity of long-context learning. Finally, we apply our findings to re-evaluate some previously proposed solutions to long-context imitation learning.

Title: Training with (Swap) Regret Loss in a Single-Layer Self-Attention Model: A Case Study on the Probability Simplex
Authors: Chanwoo Park, Asuman Ozdaglar
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: We revisit the regret loss framework introduced in Park et al. (2025), which uses decision-theoretic regret as a direct loss function for training models to make better decisions, through the lens of probability-simplex policies. Our first result shows that a single-layer self-attention model trained with regret loss admits a stationary point whose forward-pass exactly matches smoothed fictitious play with the appropriate stepsize that ensures no-regret behavior-i.e., for any given policy input, the model outputs the same update that smoothed fictitious play would produce. In parallel, we also newly introduce a swap-regret loss function, which extends the regret-loss framework beyond external regret and enables models to directly optimize for swap-deviation robustness. We further show that this swap-regret loss admits a stationary point whose forward pass implements the corresponding swap-regret update induced by classical Blum-Mansour no-pass implementation algorithm, with each head implementing an external-regret update via smoothed fictitious play. Together, these results show that regret-trained attention can realize differentiable mechanisms whose deployment induces equilibrium behavior in games: external-regret dynamics lead to coarse correlated equilibrium, while swap-regret dynamics lead to correlated equilibrium. Thus, regret-based objectives steer minimal attention architectures toward online-learning dynamics with game-theoretic guarantees, without supervised traces of those algorithms.

Title: Tree Decomposition of Product and Nest Graphs for Assortment Optimization under the Generalized Nested Logit Model
Authors: YuHeng Wang, Paat Rusmevichientong, Hüseyin Topaloğlu
Affiliations: SKEMA Business School; University of Southern California; Cornell University

Title: Truthful Fair Division under Stochastic Valuations
Authors: Daniel Halpern, Alexandros Psomas, Shirley Zhang
Affiliations: Google (United States); Harvard University
Abstract: We study no-money mechanisms for allocating indivisible items to strategic agents with additive preferences under a stochastic model. In this model, items' values are drawn from an underlying distribution and mechanisms are evaluated with respect to this draw (e.g., in expectation, or with high probability). Motivated by worst-case impossibilities which show that truthfulness severely restricts fairness and efficiency, we ask whether truthful mechanisms continue to perform poorly on random instances. We first focus on dominant-strategy incentive compatible (DSIC) mechanisms. For two agents, we obtain a tight picture. Specifically, we show that there exists a distribution under which no DSIC mechanism achieves an expected welfare approximation better than $\frac{2+\sqrt{2}}{4}\approx 0.854$, and we give a DSIC mechanism that matches this bound for all distributions simultaneously. We further show that, for every distribution, there exists a DSIC mechanism that is envy-free with high probability and obtains the same welfare. A key ingredient is a new, tight connection between welfare guarantees of a family of DSIC, no-money mechanisms and i.i.d.\ prophet inequalities. This connection allows us to generalize to $n$ agents; in particular, we obtain a DSIC mechanism that achieves a $\approx 0.745$ approximation to welfare, and another DSIC mechanism achieving a $1/2$-approximation welfare that is envy-free with high probability. We then turn to Bayesian incentive compatibility (BIC). Under i.i.d.\ valuations, we show that BIC comes at essentially no cost: we design a prior-independent BIC mechanism that achieves a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation to the optimal welfare, while being envy-free with high probability. Under independent but non-identical priors, we obtain BIC mechanisms that are $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximately Pareto efficient and envy-free with high probability.

Title: Universal Diffusion Models for Implied Volatility Surfaces: Learning Shared Dynamics Across Stocks
Authors: Mingzhi Yang, Sheng Wang, Chao Zhang, Ruikun Li
Affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Abstract: Modeling the dynamics of option implied volatility surface (IVS) is crucial for pricing, hedging, and risk-managing option portfolios. We develop a universal conditional diffusion model that learns to jointly generate next-day IVS increments and the underlying stock's returns. The model is trained on pooled data from 50 stocks and evaluated on a test set comprising 50 in-sample stocks and 50 out-of-sample stocks excluded from training. The training objective is primarily the minimization of MSE, with the variants that jointly impose surface smoothness, and that penalize the presence of static-arbitrage, which are all economically meaningful constraints. Across in-sample and out-of-sample stocks, our diffusion model outperforms the VolGAN benchmark in reducing arbitrage violations, improving stock risk prediction, and aligning explained variance ratios by the first three principal components. The fact that the model extrapolates well to stocks that are excluded from training indicates that the learned dynamics can be shared across stocks. These findings support a universal conditional diffusion as a credible framework for multi-stock implied volatility surface scenario generation.

Title: Variance-Adaptive Optimal Algorithm for Reinforcement Learning with Multinomial Logit Function Approximation
Authors: Wonyoung Kim, Min-Hwan Oh, Garud Iyengar, Assaf J. Zeevi
Affiliations: Seoul National University; Columbia University
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with multinomial logistic (MNL) function approximation has become an important framework due to its flexibility and broad applicability.
